docs.title: Filterung und Glättung
docs.text:
Rohe Sensordaten benötigen oft Filterung:

# Exponentielles Glätten
def exponential_smoothing(measurements, alpha=0.3):
    """
    Glätte Sensormessungen.

    alpha: Glättungsfaktor (0–1)
           0 = keine Glättung
           1 = nur aktueller Wert
    """
    smoothed = [measurements[0]]
    for m in measurements[1:]:
        s = alpha * m + (1 - alpha) * smoothed[-1]
        smoothed.append(s)
    return smoothed

# Moving Average
def moving_average(measurements, window=5):
    """Gleitender Durchschnitt."""
    return [
        sum(measurements[max(0, i-window):i+1]) /
        min(window, i+1)
        for i in range(len(measurements))
    ]

docs.title: Ausreißer-Erkennung
docs.text:
def detect_outliers(measurements, threshold=3.0):
    """
    Erkenne Ausreißer mit Z-Score.

    threshold: Standardabweichungen für Ausreißer-Klassifikation
    """
    mean = sum(measurements) / len(measurements)
    std = (sum((x - mean)**2 for x in measurements) / len(measurements))**0.5

    outliers = []
    for i, m in enumerate(measurements):
        z_score = abs(m - mean) / std if std > 0 else 0
        if z_score > threshold:
            outliers.append(i)

    return outliers

docs.title: pH-Regelung
docs.text:
def ph_control(ph_measurement, setpoint=7.2, tolerance=0.2):
    """
    Einfache pH-Regelung.

    Returns: Kalk-Dosierungsrate [kg/d]
    """
    error = setpoint - ph_measurement

    if error > tolerance:
        # pH zu niedrig, füge Kalk hinzu
        dosing_rate = min(100, error * 50)  # Proportionale Regelung
    elif error < -tolerance:
        # pH zu hoch, reduziere Kalk
        dosing_rate = 0
    else:
        # Innerhalb Toleranz
        dosing_rate = 0

    return dosing_rate

docs.title: Fütterungssteuerung basierend auf VFA
docs.text:
def adaptive_feeding_control(vfa_measurement, vfa_limit=4.0,
                             current_feed_rate=15.0):
    """
    Passe Fütterungsrate basierend auf VFA an.

    vfa_limit: VFA-Grenzwert [g/L]
    current_feed_rate: Aktuelle Rate [m³/d]

    Returns: Angepasste Fütterungsrate [m³/d]
    """
    if vfa_measurement > vfa_limit:
        # Übersäuerungsrisiko - reduziere Fütterung
        reduction_factor = vfa_limit / vfa_measurement
        new_rate = current_feed_rate * reduction_factor
        print(f"VFA hoch ({vfa_measurement:.2f} g/L) - Reduziere auf {new_rate:.1f} m³/d")
    elif vfa_measurement < vfa_limit * 0.5:
        # Stabil - kann Fütterung erhöhen
        increase_factor = 1.05  # 5% Erhöhung
        new_rate = min(current_feed_rate * increase_factor, 20.0)  # Max 20 m³/d
        print(f"VFA stabil ({vfa_measurement:.2f} g/L) - Erhöhe auf {new_rate:.1f} m³/d")
    else:
        # Innerhalb optimalen Bereichs
        new_rate = current_feed_rate

    return new_rate

docs.title: Alarm-System
docs.text:
class SensorAlarm:
    """Sensor-Alarmsystem."""

    def __init__(self, sensor_id, alarm_type, threshold, hysteresis=0.1):
        self.sensor_id = sensor_id
        self.alarm_type = alarm_type  # 'high', 'low', 'rate_of_change'
        self.threshold = threshold
        self.hysteresis = hysteresis
        self.is_active = False
        self.last_value = None

    def check(self, current_value):
        """Prüfe Alarmbedingung."""

        if self.alarm_type == 'high':
            if not self.is_active and current_value > self.threshold:
                self.is_active = True
                return f"ALARM: {self.sensor_id} hoch ({current_value:.2f})"
            elif self.is_active and current_value < (self.threshold - self.hysteresis):
                self.is_active = False
                return f"OK: {self.sensor_id} normal ({current_value:.2f})"

        elif self.alarm_type == 'low':
            if not self.is_active and current_value < self.threshold:
                self.is_active = True
                return f"ALARM: {self.sensor_id} niedrig ({current_value:.2f})"
            elif self.is_active and current_value > (self.threshold + self.hysteresis):
                self.is_active = False
                return f"OK: {self.sensor_id} normal ({current_value:.2f})"

        elif self.alarm_type == 'rate_of_change':
            if self.last_value is not None:
                rate = abs(current_value - self.last_value)
                if not self.is_active and rate > self.threshold:
                    self.is_active = True
                    return f"ALARM: {self.sensor_id} schnelle Änderung ({rate:.2f}/h)"
            self.last_value = current_value

        return None

# Beispielverwendung
alarms = {
    'pH_low': SensorAlarm('pH1', 'low', 6.8, hysteresis=0.1),
    'pH_high': SensorAlarm('pH1', 'high', 8.0, hysteresis=0.1),
    'VFA_high': SensorAlarm('VFA1', 'high', 4.0, hysteresis=0.5),
    'temp_deviation': SensorAlarm('T1', 'rate_of_change', 2.0)  # 2 °C/h
}

# In Simulationsschleife
for measurement in ph_measurements:
    for alarm in alarms.values():
        message = alarm.check(measurement)
        if message:
            print(message)

docs.title: Sensordaten-Protokollierung
docs.text:
import csv
from datetime import datetime

class SensorDataLogger:
    """Protokolliere Sensordaten."""

    def __init__(self, filename):
        self.filename = filename
        self.file = None
        self.writer = None

    def open(self, sensor_ids):
        """Öffne Logdatei."""
        self.file = open(self.filename, 'w', newline='')
        self.writer = csv.writer(self.file)
        # Header
        self.writer.writerow(['timestamp', 'time_days'] + sensor_ids)

    def log(self, time_days, sensor_values):
        """Protokolliere einen Zeitpunkt."""
        timestamp = datetime.now().isoformat()
        row = [timestamp, time_days] + sensor_values
        self.writer.writerow(row)

    def close(self):
        """Schließe Logdatei."""
        if self.file:
            self.file.close()

# Verwendung
logger = SensorDataLogger('sensor_data.csv')
logger.open(['pH', 'T', 'VFA', 'Q_gas', 'CH4'])

# In Simulation
for t in range(simulation_steps):
    # ... Simulation ...
    sensor_values = [
        digester.outputs_data['pH'],
        digester.T_ad,
        digester.outputs_data['VFA'],
        digester.outputs_data['Q_gas'],
        digester.outputs_data['Q_ch4']
    ]
    logger.log(t, sensor_values)

logger.close()

docs.title: Fermenter-Ausgaben als virtuelle Sensoren
docs.text:
Die Fermenter-Komponente liefert bereits Prozessindikatoren, die direkt zur Überwachung verwendet werden können — mit oder ohne dedizierte Sensorkomponenten:

from pyadm1.components.biological import Digester

# Fermenter liefert bereits Prozessindikatoren
digester = Digester("dig1", feedstock, V_liq=2000)
result = digester.step(t, dt, inputs)

# Verfügbare "Sensor"-Werte
monitoring_data = {
    'pH': result['pH'],
    'VFA': result['VFA'],            # g/L
    'TAC': result['TAC'],            # g CaCO3/L
    'Q_gas': result['Q_gas'],        # m³/d
    'Q_ch4': result['Q_ch4'],        # m³/d
    'Q_co2': result['Q_co2']         # m³/d
}

# Einfache Prozessüberwachung
if monitoring_data['pH'] < 6.8:
    print("Warnung: Niedriger pH")

if monitoring_data['VFA'] / monitoring_data['TAC'] > 0.4:
    print("Warnung: Hohes VFA/TAC-Verhältnis")

docs.title: What is PyADM1ODE?
docs.text:
PyADM1ODE is a comprehensive Python framework for agricultural biogas plant modeling that combines:

  • Scientific accuracy: Based on IWA's ADM1 model, the international standard for anaerobic digestion.
  • Modular architecture: Mix and match components (digesters, CHP units, pumps, mixers) to build any plant configuration.
  • Real-world applicability: Validated with data from operating biogas plants.
  • Python ecosystem: Integrates with NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, and visualization libraries.

docs.title: Toolbox Extensions
docs.text:
Specialized ecosystem extensions are available for advanced tasks such as parameter calibration and state estimation:

  • PyADM1ODE Calibration: Parameter calibration framework for biogas plant models. Fits ADM1 parameters to historical plant data (initial calibration) and supports continuous online recalibration during operation, along with sensitivity and identifiability analyses.
  • PyADM1ODE Estimate: Real-time state estimation for biogas plants using live sensor measurements. Employs methods such as the Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF), deep learning ensembles, and sensor fusion to estimate unmeasurable plant states as input for control algorithms and feeding recommendations.

docs.title: Quick Example
docs.text:
Build and simulate a complete biogas plant in just a few lines:

from pyadm1.configurator import BiogasPlant, PlantConfigurator
from pyadm1.substrates import Feedstock

# Create plant
feedstock = Feedstock(feeding_freq=48)
plant = BiogasPlant("My Biogas Plant")
configurator = PlantConfigurator(plant, feedstock)

# Add digester (automatically creates gas storage)
configurator.add_digester(
    digester_id="main_digester",
    V_liq=2000.0,              # 2000 m³ liquid volume
    V_gas=300.0,               # 300 m³ gas headspace
    T_ad=308.15,               # 35°C mesophilic
    Q_substrates=[15, 10, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]  # Corn silage + manure
)

# Add CHP and heating (automatically creates flare)
configurator.add_chp("chp_main", P_el_nom=500.0)
configurator.add_heating("heating_main", target_temperature=308.15)

# Connect components
configurator.auto_connect_digester_to_chp("main_digester", "chp_main")
configurator.auto_connect_chp_to_heating("chp_main", "heating_main")

# Simulate
plant.initialize()
results = plant.simulate(duration=30, dt=1/24, save_interval=1.0)

# Analyze
final = results[-1]["components"]["main_digester"]
print(f"Biogas: {final['Q_gas']:.1f} m³/d")
print(f"Methane: {final['Q_ch4']:.1f} m³/d")
print(f"pH: {final['pH']:.2f}")

docs.title: Four-Pass Simulation Step
docs.text:
Gas consumers depend on what the storages can supply, and heating systems on the heat of the CHP. BiogasPlant.step therefore runs every time step in four passes; each component is stepped exactly once.

sequenceDiagram
    participant S as BiogasPlant.step
    participant D as Digesters and feed chain
    participant G as Gas storages
    participant C as CHP / upgrading / heating
    participant F as Flares

    Note over S,F: Time Step (t -> t + dt)

    rect rgb(200, 220, 240)
    Note right of S: Pass 1: Production
    S->>D: step()
    D->>G: Produced gas
    end

    rect rgb(220, 240, 200)
    Note right of S: Pass 2: Storages
    C->>G: Gas demand
    S->>G: step() with production and demand
    Note right of G: Gas beyond capacity is vented
    end

    rect rgb(240, 220, 200)
    Note right of S: Pass 3: Consumers
    G-->>C: Gas actually supplied
    S->>C: step(), heating after the CHP
    end

    rect rgb(240, 230, 210)
    Note right of S: Pass 4: Flares
    G-->>F: Vented gas
    S->>F: step()
    end

docs.title: Benchmark Dataset
docs.text:
The benchmark dataset is a collection of described biogas plants. It is used to test how well an artificial intelligence (AI) can rebuild a working PyADM1ODE model from the description of a plant.

In a nutshell

An AI reads the description of a biogas plant – as text or as a sketch – and is supposed to rebuild that same plant in the computer. The benchmark measures how accurately it succeeds.

docs.title: What is this about?
docs.text:
PyADM1ODE is software that can simulate biogas plants. To make the software compute a specific plant, you first have to describe that plant: How many vessels are there? How big are they? How are they connected? Is there a combined heat and power unit?

Exactly this step – from a description in words to a finished plant in the software – is the task the benchmark evaluates. The AI receives a description and produces the plant from it. Its result is then compared against a known reference solution.

The graphic gives an overview of the dataset. Its individual parts are described in detail in the following sections.

docs.title: Why is this useful?
docs.text:
• Comparability: Different AI models solve the same tasks – you can objectively see which one performs better.
  • Realism: The plants are based on real agricultural biogas plants.
  • Understanding: The dataset vividly shows what a biogas plant consists of and what matters when modelling one.

docs.title: Who is this documentation for?
docs.text: This introduction is aimed at readers without programming experience. No coding knowledge is required – technical terms are explained along the way.

docs.text:
Each plant lives in its own folder. There are currently eleven example plants that differ in size and equipment:

Plant Short description BGA1 Large plant: two fermenters, secondary digester, digestate store, biogas upgrading, separator BGA2 Small plant: one fermenter, secondary digester, digestate store, combined heat and power unit BGA3 Medium plant: two fermenters, secondary digester, digestate store, combined heat and power unit BGA4 Real plant (250 kW): digester, post-digester, digestate store, combined heat and power unit BGA5 Small slurry plant (75 kW): fermenter and gas-tight digestate store only, no secondary digester BGA6 Energy-crop plant (360 kW): horizontal plug-flow digester (thermophilic), secondary digester, digestate store, separator with press-water recirculation BGA7 Flexibilised plant (800 kW): two fermenters in series, gas-tight and open digestate store, separator, two CHP units BGA8 Four-stage chain (300 kW): fermenter, two identical secondary digesters in series, digestate store, combined heat and power unit BGA9 Four-stage chain (400 kW): fermenter, secondary digester, two gas-tight digestate stores in series, combined heat and power unit BGA10 Two parallel lines (750 kW): one fermenter and one secondary digester per line, shared digestate store, combined heat and power unit — five tanks BGA11 Two gas consumers (250 kW + 350 m³/h): two fermenters, secondary digester, digestate store, combined heat and power unit and biogas upgrading in parallel

BGA = biogas plant

"BGA" simply stands for the German Biogasanlage (biogas plant). The number distinguishes the eleven examples.

docs.title: Variants: the same plant, described differently
docs.text:
For each plant there is the same biogas plant, but described in different ways. This makes it possible to test whether the AI is robust – regardless of whether the description is long, short, in English or a sketch.

Two properties are combined here:

1. The form of the description

  • detailed text – an explanatory prose description
  • terse text – only the key figures
  • English text – the same plant in English
  • sketch – a drawing of the plant (image)

2. How complete the description is

  • complete (suffix _full): All required information is in the description. The AI does not need to ask anything.
  • incomplete: Some information is missing (e.g. the operating temperature). The AI has to ask the oracle for it — a guess is practically never close enough.

For the sketch the text adds only what is missing

In the complete variant …_sketch_full the supplementary text states only what the image does not carry itself. The sketch labels dimensions and CHP power — the supplement does not repeat that, it supplies the operating temperature, the fill level, the gas space, the efficiencies and the path of the digestate. That keeps the task tied to actually reading the sketch.

Example

BGA2_terse_de_full means: plant BGA2, terse description, in German (de), with all information (full).

docs.title: The reference solution ("Gold")
docs.text: Each plant comes with a reference solution – similar to the answer sheet for a school exercise. It describes the correctly built plant and serves as the benchmark against which the AI's result is measured. All variants of a plant share the same reference solution, because it is always the same plant.

docs.title: What the folders look like
docs.text:
In simplified form, the storage layout looks like this:

Dataset/
  BGA1/                     ← plant 1 (one folder per plant)
    BGA1_text_de.json         detailed text (German), incomplete
    BGA1_text_de_full.json    detailed text (German), complete
    BGA1_text_en.json         English text
    BGA1_terse_de.json        terse description
    BGA1_sketch.json          sketch only
    BGA1_sketch.png           the sketch image
    gold.py                   the shared reference solution
  BGA2/  …                   ← plant 2 (same layout)
  BGA3/  …                   ← plant 3 (same layout)
  BGA4/  …                   ← plant 4 (same layout)
  BGA5/  …                   ← plant 5 (same layout, no secondary digester)
  BGA6/  …                   ← plant 6 (same layout, plug-flow digester)
  BGA7/  …                   ← plant 7 (same layout, two CHP units)
  BGA8/  …                   ← plant 8 (same layout, serial chain)
  BGA9/  …                   ← plant 9 (same layout, two stores)
  BGA10/ …                   ← plant 10 (same layout, two parallel lines)
  BGA11/ …                   ← plant 11 (same layout, CHP + upgrading)

What is a .json file?

A .json file is a text file in a fixed format that a computer can read easily. You can think of it as a filled-in form with clearly named fields. What exactly is in such a form is explained on the page A Data Point in Detail.

Each of these task files is what we call a data point. What is inside one is what we look at next.

docs.title: Scoring & Workflow
docs.text: This page explains how a test runs and how the score is produced – without any programming knowledge.

docs.title: The workflow of a test
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    A["📝 The AI receives the<br>plant description"] --> B{Information missing?}
    B -- "yes" --> C["❓ AI asks questions<br>– the oracle answers"]
    B -- "no" --> D["🏗️ AI builds the plant"]
    C --> D
    D --> E["🔍 The built plant is<br>compared with the reference"]
    E --> F["📊 Three scores<br>in percent"]

Step by step:

  1. Read the task: The AI receives the description (text or sketch).
  2. Ask questions (only for incomplete tasks): If something is missing, the AI may query the oracle.
  3. Build the plant: The AI creates instructions with which PyADM1ODE actually assembles the plant.
  4. Compare: The resulting plant is compared with the reference (the correct plant).
  5. Score: From this, three scores in percent are produced.

What does 'the AI builds the plant' mean?

The AI writes a short set of instructions in the language that PyADM1ODE understands. You can think of it as a blueprint: "Take a fermenter of this size, connect it to the secondary digester …". These instructions are executed, and a real, simulatable plant is created.

docs.title: The three scores
docs.text:
The result is examined from three angles. Each score is a percentage between 0 % and 100 %. The three angles are deliberately chosen so that every possible mistake maps to exactly one of them.

  • 1. Completeness

    Is everything needed there? If a vessel, a combined heat and power unit or a pipe between two components is missing, this score drops.

  • 2. Measures

    Are the sizes and values correct – such as volume, temperature or the power of the combined heat and power unit? Checking uses a tolerance range, so small deviations are allowed.

  • 3. No inventions

    Is only what belongs there actually there? If the AI adds an extra component or a pipe that does not exist, this score drops.

How tight is the tolerance range?

Every figure the simulation needs is either stated in the description or the AI can ask for it. It never has to guess. The range is tight accordingly — it only covers what is unavoidable when calculating:

  • If the value is taken over (from the description or from the oracle), the AI has to hit it. Only rounding is allowed: 40 °C as 313.0 instead of 313.15 K is fine, 39 °C is not.
  • If the value has to be calculated — a volume from diameter and height, say — slightly more deviation is allowed. Depending on where you round, results differ.

docs.title: Every mistake counts exactly once
docs.text:
What the AI gets wrong Which score drops omits a component or a pipe 1. Completeness invents a value that is not plausible 2. Measures invents a component or a pipe 3. No inventions

If the AI invents a component of a kind the plant does not have at all – a separator in a plant without any separator, say – the third score is capped hard. That is the most serious error.

Omitting does not pay off either: leaving out a component does not get rid of its pipes – they then count as missing as well.

docs.title: What counts – and what does not
docs.text:
To keep the scoring fair and meaningful, some things are deliberately not scored:

  • Names do not matter: The AI may name components differently. Comparison is by type of component (fermenter, pump …), not by name.
  • Substrates are not scored: Which materials are fed in does not factor into the score – it is solely about the structure of the plant.
  • Asking questions is not graded: Whether the AI asks is up to it. Only the plant it finally produces is scored — guessing wrong costs points on Measures.

docs.title: Note on sketch tasks
docs.text: Tasks with a sketch (image) can only be solved by AI models that understand images. A pure text model cannot "see" a sketch and would inevitably score 0 % on such tasks – this is then not a content error of the model, but a question of choosing the right model. Whether a model accepts images is usually reported by the API itself; on Groq, for instance, as input_modalities.

docs.title: A Data Point in Detail
docs.text:
A data point is a single task for the AI. It contains everything needed for that task: the description of the plant, the correct solution for comparison, and a few additional details for fair scoring.

This page explains the components in plain language.

docs.title: The four main components
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    DP["📄 Data point"] --> E["1) Input<br>the task"]
    DP --> R["2) Reference<br>the correct plant"]
    DP --> O["3) Oracle<br>answers questions"]
    DP --> Z["4) Regime<br>complete or not"]

docs.title: 1. The input – the actual task
docs.text: This is the description of the plant that the AI gets to see. Depending on the variant, it is a detailed text, a terse text or a sketch (image). The AI receives only this input – nothing else.

docs.title: 2. The reference – the correct plant
docs.text:
The reference describes what the plant should correctly look like. It is the "ground truth" against which the AI's result is measured. It consists of two lists:

  • Components: all vessels and devices (e.g. fermenter, secondary digester, digestate store, combined heat and power unit) with their key data such as size and temperature.
  • Connections: who is connected to whom – that is, where the digestate flows and where the biogas is routed.

A plant as components + connections (BGA2)

flowchart LR
    F1["Fermenter F1"] -->|digestate| N1["Secondary digester N1"]
    N1 -->|digestate| G1["Digestate store G1"]
    F1 -.biogas.-> BHKW["Combined heat & power"]
    N1 -.biogas.-> BHKW
    G1 -.biogas.-> BHKW

docs.title: 3. The oracle – the expert for follow-up questions
docs.text:
Some descriptions are deliberately incomplete – just like in practice, where not all information is always available. So that the AI can still proceed, there is the oracle: a kind of expert that the AI may ask specific questions when something is unclear.

If the AI asks, for example, "At what temperature does the fermenter run?", the oracle provides the correct answer (e.g. "40 °C"). The oracle also recognises different phrasings of the same question.

Besides single values it answers questions about the plant flow: where the digestate goes, and which tanks feed the CHP or the upgrading unit. Tasks that are described completely have no oracle at all — everything is in the input there.

Why is there an oracle?

It is meant to distinguish two behaviours: a good AI asks when information is missing. A weaker AI simply guesses – and may get it wrong.

docs.title: 4. The regime – complete or incomplete
docs.text:
The regime describes whether the task is fully described or not:

  • fully specified: All information is in the description. No asking needed.
  • underspecified: Information is missing and has to be asked of the oracle.

There is no separate list of prohibitions. What the AI must not invent follows directly from the reference: a plant whose reference contains no separator simply must not contain one — the no-inventions score checks that against the reference itself.

docs.title: How "certain" a piece of information is
docs.text:
Not every detail is equally unambiguous. Therefore, each property records where it comes from:

Classification Meaning given Stated directly in the description. derivable Can be computed from other information (e.g. a volume from height and diameter). may be asked Missing – the AI has to ask the oracle; the tolerance band is too tight to guess the value. automatic Created on its own during assembly (e.g. a gas storage for each fermenter).

This allows fair scoring later on: the AI may fill in a missing value without it counting as an error straight away – as long as the addition is plausible.

docs.title: A worked example: the gas storage volume
docs.text:
A vivid example is the gas space of a vessel. It is made up of two parts:

  1. the dome roof, which sits on top of the vessel and serves as gas storage, and
  2. the unfilled headspace – the part of the vessel deliberately left without liquid (typically around 10 %).

In the complete descriptions, the total gas space is stated directly, so the AI does not have to derive it itself.

How a score is finally produced from all this information is explained on the next page: Scoring & Workflow.

docs.title: Using the Dataset
docs.text:
This page is for users of the dataset, for example to evaluate or train your own model. It explains what the dataset contains, what you run, and how to plug in your own model.

The notebook benchmark/llm_benchmark_en.ipynb provides a simple introduction to using the dataset:

docs.title: Getting the dataset
docs.text:
The dataset is part of the repository under benchmark/. No separate download is required:

git clone https://github.com/dgaida/PyADM1ODE.git
cd PyADM1ODE

The PyADM1ODE environment is needed to run code (the biogas conda environment is recommended). Pure graph scoring (matcher.py) and the viewer work without PyADM1ODE.

docs.title: What it contains
docs.text:
benchmark/
  schema/    plant_datapoint.schema.json   JSON schema (Draft 2020-12) of a data point
  dataset/   index.json                    manifest of all data points
             BGA1/ BGA2/ ...               one plant each, input variants + gold.py
  eval/      solve.py runner.py matcher.py batch.py make_index.py validate.py …
  viewer/    index.html                    interactive data point viewer

One folder per plant. It holds all input variants plus a shared gold solution gold.py (correct PyADM1ODE code).

File Role BGAx_<variant>.json Task: input (text or image) for the model and the reference plant (typed graph) for comparison gold.py Gold solution: known-correct implementation, validates the harness and serves as reference code

docs.title: Variants and regime
docs.text:
Each plant exists in several variants. The _full suffix marks completeness:

  • fully_specified (_full): all data is in the input – no oracle needed.
  • underspecified (no _full): values are missing – the model has to ask the oracle. Guessing does not work; the acceptance bands are too tight for that.
Axis Values Distribution (88) Plant BGA1 … BGA11 8 each Completeness fully_specified / underspecified 44 / 44 Modality text / image / hybrid 66 / 11 / 11 Language de / en 66 / 22

The exact makeup of a single data point is described in A Data Point in Detail. The authoritative format lives in the JSON schema at benchmark/schema/plant_datapoint.schema.json.

docs.title: What you run
docs.text:
Goal Command Matcher self-test (without PyADM1ODE) python benchmark/eval/selftest.py Validate data points against the schema python benchmark/eval/validate.py Baseline – all data points with gold.py python benchmark/eval/batch.py One data point: run code + score python benchmark/eval/runner.py <datapoint.json> <code.py> Score the graph only (no code run) python benchmark/eval/matcher.py <datapoint.json> <candidate.json> LLM evaluation python benchmark/eval/solve.py [filters] Refresh viewer/index python benchmark/eval/make_index.py

Examples:

# 1) Quick functional check of the matcher (no PyADM1ODE needed)
python benchmark/eval/selftest.py

# 2) Baseline: score all 88 data points against their gold.py
python benchmark/eval/batch.py

# 3) Run and score a single data point with the gold solution
python benchmark/eval/runner.py \
    benchmark/dataset/BGA1/BGA1_text_de.json benchmark/dataset/BGA1/gold.py

batch.py writes benchmark/results.csv. solve.py stores a CSV plus the generated code per data point under benchmark/results/.

docs.title: Plugging in or training your own model
docs.text:
The input is in the data point under input (fields modality, language, content, optionally image_path or document_path). The target is runnable PyADM1ODE code that builds the plant. The reference for comparison is under reference (components + connections as a typed graph). gold.py shows a correct implementation per plant.

The quickest path is interactively in the notebook. For automated runs there are two scripted ways (A and B).

docs.title: A) Generate code offline, then score
docs.text:
Have your model produce Python code per data point and save it as <datapoint-id>.py in a folder. Then:

python benchmark/eval/batch.py --candidates path/to/model_outputs

batch.py runs each candidate in isolation and scores it.

docs.title: B) Directly via solve.py (API)
docs.text:
solve.py is a full run including oracle rounds. By default it uses the Groq API. For your own model, only the client section in solve.py needs adapting; the rest of the workflow (prompt, oracle, scoring) stays the same.

pip install -e ".[benchmark]"   # groq; or your own client library
export GROQ_API_KEY=...    # or your own API key
python benchmark/eval/solve.py --regime fully_specified   # simplest entry point

docs.title: Follow-up questions on underspecified data points
docs.text:
If a value is missing, the model may ask first — as a JSON block with open_questions (format see prompt.py). solve.py forwards the questions to the oracle and sends the answers in a second turn.

The questions themselves are not graded. Only the plant that finally comes out is scored: not asking and still hitting plausible values costs nothing — not asking and getting it wrong costs points on Measures.

docs.title: Programmatic access
docs.text:
The manifest dataset/index.json lists all data points with id, path, language, modality, regime:

import json
from pathlib import Path

root = Path("benchmark/dataset")
index = json.loads((root / "index.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

for entry in index["datapoints"]:
    dp = json.loads((root / entry["path"]).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    task = dp["input"]["content"]        # description for the model
    reference = dp["reference"]          # target plant (components + connections)
    # ... call your own model, generate code, score ...

docs.title: Scoring
docs.text:
Three scores are computed, deliberately disjoint — every mistake counts exactly once:

  1. Completeness – are all required components and connections present?
  2. Measures – simulated parameters (V_liq, V_gas, T_ad, P_el_nom, …) within the acceptance band.
  3. No inventions – does the plant contain only components and connections the reference knows?

How the final score is produced is explained in Scoring & Workflow. You can explore the dataset visually in the Viewer.

docs.title: How does the Oracle work?
docs.text:
Some plant descriptions are deliberately incomplete – just like in practice, where not all information is always available. So that the AI can still proceed, there is the oracle: a simulated expert that the AI may ask specific questions when something is unclear. This page explains when the oracle is active, how a question turns into an answer and why that matters for fair scoring.

For a first introduction see A Data Point in Detail; this page is about the mechanism behind it.

docs.title: When is the oracle active?
docs.text:
The oracle is consulted only for under-specified tasks:

  • fully specified (fully_specified): all information is in the description. There is nothing to ask – the oracle stays silent.
  • under-specified (underspecified): values are missing. Only here may the AI ask follow-up questions, and only then does the oracle answer.

Basis: the oracle field

Every data point carries an oracle field – a dictionary of field name → value. It is the expert's only source of knowledge. Example (shortened):

"oracle": {
  "F1.T_ad": 313.15,
  "G1.T_ad": 293.15,
  "F1.fill_fraction": 0.9,
  "bgaa.exists": true,
  "chp.exists": false,
  "sep.source": "N1",
  "substrate_feed": "approx. 80 t/d maize silage and 20 m³/d cattle slurry"
}

docs.title: The two-round workflow
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    A["📝 Input<br>(incomplete)"] --> B["🤖 AI – round 1"]
    B --> C{"Code already<br>written?"}
    C -->|"yes"| Z["⚖️ Scoring"]
    C -->|"no, asks questions"| D["🔮 Oracle<br>answers the questions"]
    D --> E["🤖 AI – round 2<br>writes the code"]
    E --> Z

  1. Round 1: the AI receives the description. For under-specified tasks it may emit its open questions as a small JSON block instead of guessing immediately:

    { "open_questions": [{ "field": "F1.T_ad" }, { "field": "sep.source" }] }

  2. Oracle: if the AI asks questions (and does not yet supply code), the oracle looks up the matching values in the oracle field and returns them as an answer.

  3. Round 2: with the answers in hand, the AI writes the full PyADM1ODE code, which is then scored.

If the AI already writes finished code in round 1, the oracle round is skipped. There is at most one oracle round per data point (oracle_turns in the result).

docs.title: How a question becomes an answer
docs.text:
The oracle understands different phrasings of the same question. You do not have to hit the internal field F1.T_ad – "At what temperature does the fermenter run?" is enough. Matching runs in several stages, from the most precise to the most generous:

Stage What happens Example 1. Exact match The question names the field directly. F1.T_ad → 313.15 2. Keywords Synonyms are mapped to a quantity. "temperature", "heated", "mesophilic" → all *.T_ad 3. Component IDs A named component returns all of its fields. "F1" → F1.T_ad, F1.V_gas, F1.fill_fraction 4. Literal fields Field names appearing in the text are added. "… bgaa.capacity_m3h …"

The keyword table is bilingual (German and English) and covers typical terms – for example "gas storage"/"Gasspeicher" for V_gas, "fill level"/"Füllgrad" for fill_fraction, "rated power"/"Nennleistung" for P_el_nom or "feedstock"/"Substrat" for substrate_feed. Terms such as "efficiency" deliberately return both related fields (eta_el and eta_th).

Question → oracle answer

The AI asks:

{ "open_questions": [{ "field": "operating temperature of the fermenters" }] }

The oracle replies:

Antworten auf deine Fragen:

- F1.T_ad: 313.15  
- F2.T_ad: 313.15  
- N1.T_ad: 313.15  
- G1.T_ad: 293.15  

Bitte schreibe nun den vollständigen Python-Code.

docs.title: Helpful, but not omniscient
docs.text:
The oracle is deliberately cooperative:

  • No matching question recognised? Then it would rather hand out all available information than leave the AI stuck.
  • Only a little asked? If the AI asked for only a small part and at most five other fields remain open, the oracle adds them as "further relevant information". A run thus does not fail because of a single forgotten question.

docs.title: Why the oracle exists
docs.text:
The oracle separates two behaviours that would otherwise be indistinguishable:

  • A good AI asks when information is missing – and then builds the plant correctly.
  • A weaker AI guesses and may invent an implausible value.

This is exactly what the scoring reflects — but indirectly: the questions themselves are not graded. A model that asks gets the right values and lands inside the acceptance band on Measures; one that guesses wrong loses points there. See Scoring & Workflow for the details.

docs.title: Turning the oracle off
docs.text:
For comparison the oracle can be disabled. The AI then asks no follow-up questions and has to guess the missing values:

python benchmark/eval/solve.py --no-oracle

This is the counter-check to the regular run: it shows what asking is actually worth. Expect the Measures score to drop sharply — the acceptance bands are far too tight to guess a value that was never stated.

You can explore the dataset visually – including the oracle answers per data point – in the Viewer.

docs.title: Data Point Viewer
docs.text: The viewer (benchmark/viewer/index.html) shows each data point interactively (the input, the oracle answers, metadata and the parameters of every component). Ideal for exploring the dataset and understanding a plant. It runs offline in the browser, with no server.

docs.title: What the viewer shows
docs.text:
• Plant graph: components as nodes, connections as edges.
  • Component details: a table of the simulated parameters, acceptance band and notes.
  • Sidebar: the input, the oracle answers and the metadata.

docs.title: Legend (graph)
docs.text:
Element Meaning Node color component type (Digester, GasStorage, CHP, Flare, …) Edge color / style connection type: liquid · gas · heat Node border the component's obligation (given / derivable / may-be-asked / automatic)

The legend in the lower-left of the viewer summarises the color coding.

docs.title: Launching
docs.text: You can run the viewer offline, but new changes to the dataset will not be shown. Alternatively, refresh the index file or start a local server to see changes directly in the viewer.

docs.title: Offline
docs.text: Double-clicking benchmark/viewer/index.html opens the viewer directly (file://). It then shows an embedded copy of the data points. Use Load files… to open arbitrary data point JSONs manually.

docs.title: Live mode
docs.text:
Always shows the current dataset; changes appear after a reload.

python -m http.server 8000              # simple local server

Then open in the browser: http://localhost:8000/benchmark/viewer/

docs.title: Controls
docs.text: Action Control Previous / next data point ◀ / ▶ buttons or arrow keys ←/→ Show component details click a node in the graph Zoom + / − / ⤢ buttons or mouse wheel Open your own data points Load files… (one or more .json)

docs.title: After changing the dataset
docs.text:
If you added or changed data points, regenerate the index:

python benchmark/eval/make_index.py

More about the dataset and the evaluation scripts is in Using the Dataset.

docs.title: Docstring Style Guide
docs.text: PyADM1ODE follows the Google Python Style Guide for docstrings. This ensures consistent, readable, and automatically parseable documentation.

docs.title: General Format
docs.text:
def function(arg1: int, arg2: str) -> bool:
    """
    Summary line.

    Extended description of the function and its behavior.

    Args:
        arg1: Description of arg1.
        arg2: Description of arg2.

    Returns:
        Description of the return value.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If arg1 is negative.
    """

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
class MyClass:
    """
    Summary line.

    Extended description.

    Attributes:
        attr1: Description of attr1.
    """

docs.title: Tools
docs.text: We use interrogate to enforce docstring coverage and mkdocstrings to generate the API reference. Current threshold is 95%.

docs.title: Basic Digester Example
docs.text: The example examples/01_basic_digester.py is the simplest PyADM1ODE configuration: a single digester fed with three substrates, together with the gas storage the configurator creates for it. The Colab notebook runs a shortened variant (two substrates, a larger digester, 5 days), so its numbers differ from the ones on this page.

docs.title: System Architecture
docs.text:
graph LR
    %% Substrate input
    Feed[Substrate Feed<br/>Maize silage: 11.4 t/d<br/>Swine manure: 6.1 t/d<br/>Cattle manure: 5.0 t/d] --> Digester

    %% Main digester
    Digester[Digester<br/>V_liq: 1050 m³<br/>V_gas: 150 m³<br/>T: 42 °C]

    %% Separate gas storage component
    Digester -->|Dry biogas<br/>~1960 Nm³/d<br/>CH₄ ~53 %| Storage[Gas Storage<br/>main_digester_storage<br/>Membrane type<br/>Capacity: 150 m³]

    %% No gas consumer in this example
    Storage -.->|Overflow<br/>when full| Vent[Vented<br/>no gas consumer connected]

    %% Liquid output
    Digester -->|Effluent<br/>21.2 m³/d| Effluent[Digestate Output]

    %% Styling
    classDef processBox fill:#e1f5fe,stroke:#01579b,stroke-width:2px
    classDef storageBox fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px
    classDef inputBox fill:#f1f8e9,stroke:#33691e,stroke-width:2px
    classDef outputBox fill:#fce4ec,stroke:#880e4f,stroke-width:2px

    class Digester processBox
    class Storage storageBox
    class Feed inputBox
    class Effluent,Vent outputBox

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The example shows:

  • Choosing substrates from the bundled library by ID and giving the mix as a dict {substrate_id: feed rate}
  • Building a single-digester plant with PlantConfigurator
  • The gas storage that add_digester() creates as a separate component
  • Starting from an initial state derived from the substrate mix, without a state file
  • Simulating 150 days in daily steps
  • Printing biogas, methane, methane content and pH for every tenth day
  • Saving the plant with its final state to JSON

docs.title: Plant Configuration
docs.text:
Component ID Settings Digester main_digester 1050 m³ liquid volume, 150 m³ gas headspace, 42 °C (315.15 K) Gas storage main_digester_storage Membrane type, 150 m³ capacity; created by add_digester()

The substrate feed is the DEFAULT_FEED of the script:

Substrate ID Material Feed rate maize_silage_milk_ripeness Maize silage (milk ripeness) 11.4 t/d swine_manure Pig slurry 6.1 t/d cattle_manure Cattle slurry 5.0 t/d Total 22.5 t/d

Unit of the feed rates: With the default Feedstock convention (simba_q_convention=True) the feed rates are tonnes of fresh matter per day (t FM/d). For the two slurries (density 1000 kg/m³) a tonne is a cubic metre; the 11.4 t/d of maize silage (density 1129 kg/m³) take up 10.1 m³/d. The digester therefore receives 21.2 m³/d, and the hydraulic retention time is 1050 m³ ÷ 21.2 m³/d ≈ 49.5 d. See Volumetric ADM1da convention for Q.

Gas storage: The digester has no gas storage of its own; V_gas is only the headspace of the ADM1 gas phase. add_digester() adds a separate GasStorage component named <digester_id>_storage, here main_digester_storage, and connects it to the digester with a gas connection. Its capacity is max(50, V_gas), here 150 m³. The example has no CHP or other gas consumer, so nothing is drawn from the storage: it is full after the first day and vents the whole production from then on (see Configuration Export). The component is described under Gas Storage.

docs.title: Code Walkthrough
docs.text: The excerpts are taken from the script.

docs.title: 1. Substrate Mix
docs.text:
# Default substrate mix [t FM/d] — maize silage + swine + cattle manure.
DEFAULT_FEED: dict[str, float] = {
    "maize_silage_milk_ripeness": 11.4,
    "swine_manure": 6.1,
    "cattle_manure": 5.0,
}

Each key is the ID of a substrate file under data/substrates/, which is the file name without extension (see Example Substrates). Any number of substrates may be listed. main(feed=...) accepts another mapping of the same form and splits it into two lists:

substrate_ids = list(feed.keys())
Q_substrates = list(feed.values())

docs.title: 2. Feedstock and Plant
docs.text:
from pyadm1 import BiogasPlant, Feedstock
from pyadm1.configurator.plant_configurator import PlantConfigurator

feedstock = Feedstock(substrate_ids, feeding_freq=24, total_simtime=160)
plant = BiogasPlant("ADM1 Basic Plant")
cfg = PlantConfigurator(plant, feedstock)
  • Feedstock loads the listed substrates and computes the ADM1 influent from their laboratory values. feeding_freq is the time between feeding events in hours, total_simtime the length of its time grid in days.
  • BiogasPlant is the container for all components and their connections.
  • PlantConfigurator adds components with defaults and connects them.

docs.title: 3. Digester
docs.text:
cfg.add_digester(
    digester_id="main_digester",
    V_liq=1050.0,
    V_gas=150.0,
    T_ad=315.15,
    Q_substrates=Q_substrates,
    k_L_a=200.0,
)
plant.initialize()
Argument Value Meaning V_liq 1050 m³ Liquid volume V_gas 150 m³ Gas headspace T_ad 315.15 K Operating temperature (42 °C) Q_substrates [11.4, 6.1, 5.0] Feed rates, in the order of the substrate IDs k_L_a 200 d⁻¹ Gas–liquid mass-transfer coefficient

The volumes and the temperature equal the defaults of add_digester(), and 200 d⁻¹ is also the model default of k_L_a.

add_digester() does three things:

  • It creates the digester and derives its initial state from the feedstock: a pre-inoculated state at pH 7 with active biomass, built for this substrate mix and feed rate. No state file is needed.
  • It creates the gas storage main_digester_storage.
  • It connects digester and storage with a gas connection.

It returns the digester and a one-line description of the initial state; the script does not use the return value. plant.initialize() initializes every component that is not initialized yet.

docs.title: 4. Simulation
docs.text:
results = plant.simulate(duration=150.0, dt=1.0, save_interval=1.0)
  • duration: simulated time [d]
  • dt: plant time step [d]. In every step the digester is computed first, then the gas storage receives its production. Within the step the digester integrates the ADM1 equations with SciPy's BDF solver and an adaptive step size.
  • save_interval: spacing of the saved results [d]

results holds 150 entries, one per day, with time from 1.0 to 150.0. Each entry has the form {"time": ..., "components": {component_id: outputs}}.

docs.title: 5. Report
docs.text:
times = np.array([r["time"] for r in results])
dig = [r["components"]["main_digester"] for r in results]
q_gas = np.array([c["Q_gas"] for c in dig])
q_ch4 = np.array([c["Q_ch4"] for c in dig])
pH = np.array([c["pH"] for c in dig])

Q_gas and Q_ch4 are dry gas at standard conditions (0 °C, 1.01325 bar), in Nm³/d; the water vapour of the headspace is not part of them. See Reported gas flows.

# The first saved result is the end of day 1; then every tenth day and the last.
for day in sorted({int(times[0]), *range(10, int(times[-1]) + 1, 10), int(times[-1])}):
    i = int(np.argmin(np.abs(times - day)))
    ch4p = q_ch4[i] / q_gas[i] * 100.0 if q_gas[i] > 0.0 else 0.0
    print(f"{day:>5d}  {q_gas[i]:>10.1f}  {q_ch4[i]:>10.1f}  {ch4p:>6.1f}  {pH[i]:>6.2f}")

The table has one row for the end of day 1, for every tenth day and for the last day. The column CH4% is Q_ch4 / Q_gas, the methane content of the dry gas. There is no result for day 0, because the first one is saved after the first step.

docs.title: 6. Saving
docs.text:
output_path = REPO_ROOT / "output"
output_path.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
plant.to_json(str(output_path / "quickstart_config.json"))

return plant, results

docs.title: Interpreting the Output
docs.text:
Quantity Value at day 150 Obtained from Biogas (dry) 1959.7 Nm³/d Q_gas Methane 1039.2 Nm³/d Q_ch4 Methane content of the dry gas 53.0 % Q_ch4 / Q_gas pH 7.45 pH Biogas per tonne of fresh matter 87.1 Nm³/t 1959.7 Nm³/d ÷ 22.5 t/d Methane per tonne of fresh matter 46.2 Nm³/t 1039.2 Nm³/d ÷ 22.5 t/d

Course over the 150 days:

  • Start: The first row (end of day 1) shows 1765.6 Nm³/d of biogas with 49.3 % methane. At day 10 the methane content is 53.3 %.
  • Biogas: It rises to 1959.7 Nm³/d by day 70 and stays there.
  • Methane: It reaches 1040.9 Nm³/d at day 50 and settles at 1039.2 Nm³/d. The methane content drifts from 53.3 % to 53.0 %.
  • pH: It rises from 7.38 to 7.46 and stays between 7.45 and 7.46 from day 30 on.

docs.title: More Values in the Results
docs.text:
Every saved entry holds the complete output of both components. They can be read at the end of main() or from its return value:

last = results[-1]["components"]
digester = last["main_digester"]
storage = last["main_digester_storage"]

print(digester["VFA"], digester["TAC"], digester["HRT"])
print(storage["stored_volume_m3"], storage["vented_volume_m3"])
Key Meaning Value at day 150 Q_co2 Carbon dioxide, dry [Nm³/d] 920.5 VFA Volatile fatty acids [g HAc-eq/L] 2.60 TAC Acid capacity [g CaCO₃/L] 6.78 TS Total solids [% FM] 10.6 HRT Filtered hydraulic retention time [d] 47.1 Q_out Effluent [m³/d] 21.2

HRT follows a first-order lag towards the 49.5 d given above and has reached 47.1 d at day 150.

Gas flow and pH look settled after 70 days, the acids are not: VFA rises from 0.24 g/L at the end of day 1 to 1.96 g/L at day 100 and 2.60 g/L at day 150, while TAC falls from 7.40 to 6.78 g CaCO₃/L. Within the 150 days the digester has therefore not reached a full steady state. Typical operating ranges of these indicators are listed under Process Monitoring.

from pyadm1 import BiogasPlant, Feedstock

feedstock = Feedstock(
    ["maize_silage_milk_ripeness", "swine_manure", "cattle_manure"],
    feeding_freq=24,
    total_simtime=160,
)
plant = BiogasPlant.from_json("output/quickstart_config.json", feedstock)

docs.title: Adapting the Example
docs.text:
• Substrate mix: Edit DEFAULT_FEED or pass another dict to main(feed=...). Entries can be added or removed; every key has to be a substrate ID of the library.
  • Digester: Change V_liq, V_gas or T_ad in cfg.add_digester(...). T_ad is given in Kelvin.
  • Duration and time step: Change duration, dt and save_interval in plant.simulate(...), for example dt=1.0 / 24.0 for hourly plant steps.
  • Further outputs: Read VFA, TAC or the storage values from results, see More Values in the Results.
  • Gas utilisation: Add a CHP and a heating system, see Two-Stage Plant and Energy Components.

docs.title: Parallel Simulation Example
docs.text:
The examples/05_parallel_two_stage_simulation.py example runs many simulations of one digester side by side: a comparison of four feed rates, a sweep over one kinetic parameter and a Monte Carlo analysis. All three use ParallelSimulator from pyadm1.simulation.parallel.

Despite its file name, the script simulates a single digester (one ADM1 model), not a two-stage plant.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The example shows:

  • Base model: one ADM1 model with two substrates that serves as the template for every scenario
  • Parallel scenarios: four feed rates, simulated in four worker processes
  • Parameter sweep: five values of the maximum acetate uptake rate k_m_ac, given as factors of the rate the model uses
  • Monte Carlo analysis: 50 random draws of k_m_ac from a normal distribution around that rate
  • Summary statistics: mean, standard deviation, minimum, maximum and median over the draws

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
graph TB
    subgraph "Main Process"
        Config[Scenario list]
        Results[Result list]
    end

    subgraph "Worker Pool (4 processes)"
        W1[Worker 1]
        W2[Worker 2]
        W3[Worker 3]
        W4[Worker 4]
    end

    Config -->|Scenario 1| W1
    Config -->|Scenario 2| W2
    Config -->|Scenario 3| W3
    Config -->|Scenario 4| W4

    W1 -->|Result 1| Results
    W2 -->|Result 2| Results
    W3 -->|Result 3| Results
    W4 -->|Result 4| Results

    style Config fill:#e1f5fe
    style Results fill:#c8e6c9
    style W1 fill:#fff3e0
    style W2 fill:#fff3e0
    style W3 fill:#fff3e0
    style W4 fill:#fff3e0

run_scenarios first checks the keys of every scenario and then starts a pool of n_workers processes. The base model object itself is not sent to the workers. The simulator sends its configuration instead:

  • liquid volume, gas volume and temperature (V_liq, V_gas, T_ad)
  • the substrate parameters of the feedstock, its feeding frequency and its Q convention
  • the calibration parameters that are set on the base model

Each worker builds its own Feedstock and ADM1 from this configuration, applies the scenario on top, simulates duration days and returns a ScenarioResult. The results come back in the order of the scenario list.

docs.title: Running the Example
docs.text:
python examples/05_parallel_two_stage_simulation.py

The script takes no arguments, prints its results to the console and writes no files.

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
• Feed rates are tonnes of fresh matter per day [t FM/d] under the default Feedstock convention (simba_q_convention=True). The model converts them to volume flows with the density of each substrate: 11.4 t FM/d of maize silage are 10.1 m³/d at 1129 kg/m³, and 6.1 t FM/d of swine manure (1000 kg/m³) are 6.1 m³/d. See the section "Volumetric ADM1da convention for Q" in ADM1 Implementation.
  • Gas flows (Q_gas, Q_ch4, Q_co2) are dry gas at standard conditions (0 °C, 1.01325 bar) in Nm³/d. See the section "Reported gas flows" on the same page.

docs.title: 1. Base Model
docs.text:
duration = 30.0  # days

feedstock = Feedstock(["maize_silage_milk_ripeness", "swine_manure"])
base_feed = [11.4, 6.1]  # t FM/d: maize silage, swine manure

adm1 = ADM1(feedstock, V_liq=1200.0, V_gas=216.0, T_ad=315.15)

initial_state = get_state_zero_from_csv(str(REPO_ROOT / "data" / "initial_states" / "digester_initial8.csv"))

# The workers rebuild the model from the configuration of this base model.
# The feed is not part of it: every scenario brings its own "Q".
parallel = ParallelSimulator(adm1, n_workers=4, verbose=True)
  • Feedstock: maize silage and swine manure from the substrate library. A feed vector has one entry per substrate, in the order of this list.
  • ADM1: a digester with 1200 m³ liquid volume and 216 m³ gas volume at 315.15 K (42 °C).
  • initial_state: the 41 state variables from data/initial_states/digester_initial8.csv. Every scenario starts from this state.
  • ParallelSimulator: four worker processes. Without n_workers the simulator uses the number of CPU cores minus one. verbose=True prints the progress lines shown under Output.

docs.title: 2. Feed-Rate Comparison
docs.text:
feed_scenarios = [
    ("Low Feed", [8.0, 4.0]),
    ("Base Feed", base_feed),
    ("High Feed", [15.0, 8.0]),
    ("Very High Feed", [20.0, 10.0]),
]
scenarios = [{"Q": Q} for _, Q in feed_scenarios]

results = parallel.run_scenarios(
    scenarios=scenarios,
    duration=duration,
    initial_state=initial_state,
)

A scenario is a dictionary. These keys are allowed:

Key Meaning Q Feed rates per substrate [t FM/d] T_ad Digester temperature [K]; replaces the temperature of the base model for this scenario k_dis_PS, k_dis_PF, k_hyd_ch, k_hyd_pr, k_hyd_li Disintegration and hydrolysis rates k_m_su, k_m_aa, k_m_fa, k_m_c4, k_m_pro, k_m_ac, k_m_h2 Maximum uptake rates k_p, k_L_a, K_H_co2, K_H_ch4, K_H_h2 Gas outlet, gas-liquid transfer and Henry constants

Any other key, for example k_dis or Y_su, raises a ValueError before a simulation starts. A misspelt name would otherwise be ignored, and every scenario of a sweep would return the same result.

Scenarios do not inherit a feed from the base model. A scenario without Q is simulated without feed, which is why the sweep and the Monte Carlo analysis below pass Q as a fixed parameter.

The other arguments of run_scenarios:

  • duration: simulated time per scenario [d], here 30 days
  • initial_state: start state of every scenario
  • compute_metrics: computes the values listed under Result Objects from the final state (default True)

docs.title: 3. Parameter Sweep
docs.text:
A rate given in a scenario replaces the rate of the model as it is. The model keeps k_m_ac at 8.0 d⁻¹ for 35 °C and corrects it to the operating temperature, which gives 11.76 d⁻¹ at the 42 °C of this example. The simulator applies no such correction to a scenario value. The script therefore reads the rate the model uses and builds the sweep from factors of it:

K_M_AC_SWEEP_FACTORS = [0.15, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5]

k_m_ac_nominal = nominal_rate(adm1, "k_m_ac")
print(f"   k_m_ac of the model at {adm1.T_ad - 273.15:.0f} °C: {k_m_ac_nominal:.2f} 1/d")

sweep_config = ParameterSweepConfig(
    parameter_name="k_m_ac",
    values=[factor * k_m_ac_nominal for factor in K_M_AC_SWEEP_FACTORS],
    other_params={"Q": base_feed},
)

sweep_results = parallel.parameter_sweep(
    config=sweep_config,
    duration=duration,
    initial_state=initial_state,
)

nominal_rate is a small helper of the script. It returns a calibration value if one is set on the base model, and otherwise the rate corrected to the temperature of the base model:

calibration = adm1.get_calibration_parameters()
if name in calibration:
    return float(calibration[name])
rates = ADMParams.apply_temperature_corrections(
    ADMParams.get_kinetic_params(),
    ADMParams.get_temperature_factors(),
    adm1.T_ad,
)
return float(rates[name])

parameter_sweep creates one scenario per value: a copy of other_params plus the swept parameter. Further keyword arguments are passed on to run_scenarios. The script then prints one row per successful scenario and names the one with the highest methane flow.

docs.title: 4. Monte Carlo Analysis
docs.text:
K_M_AC_REL_STD = 0.10

mc_config = MonteCarloConfig(
    n_samples=50,
    parameter_distributions={"k_m_ac": (k_m_ac_nominal, K_M_AC_REL_STD * k_m_ac_nominal)},
    fixed_params={"Q": base_feed},
    seed=42,
)

mc_results = parallel.monte_carlo(
    config=mc_config,
    duration=duration,
    initial_state=initial_state,
)
summary = parallel.summarize_results(mc_results)
  • parameter_distributions: mean and standard deviation of a normal distribution per parameter, here the rate of the model and 10 % of it. Other distributions are not available, and the draws are not truncated, so choose mean and standard deviation such that the values stay physically meaningful.
  • fixed_params: keys that are the same in every sample
  • seed: seeds the random generator of NumPy, so every run draws the same 50 values
  • summarize_results: returns n_scenarios, n_successful, n_failed and success_rate, and under metrics the statistics mean, std, min, max, median, q25 and q75 for every metric over the successful scenarios. std is the population standard deviation (np.std).

docs.title: Result Objects
docs.text:
Every scenario returns a ScenarioResult:

Field Content scenario_id Position in the scenario list, starting at 0 parameters The scenario dictionary success True if the simulation finished duration Simulated time [d] final_state State vector at the end (41 values) time_series Only with save_time_series=True: the last ten values of Q_gas, Q_ch4 and pH (pH rounded to one decimal), stored once per dt step metrics Values computed from the final state, see below error Exception type, message and traceback of a failed scenario execution_time Wall-clock time of the scenario in its worker [s]

metrics holds these values:

Key Unit Meaning Q_gas Nm³/d Dry biogas Q_ch4 Nm³/d Methane Q_co2 Nm³/d Carbon dioxide p_gas bar Sum of the dry partial pressures of hydrogen, methane and carbon dioxide CH4_content - Q_ch4 / Q_gas, the methane fraction of the dry gas pH - pH from the charge balance Q_total t FM/d Sum of the feed rates of the scenario as entered specific_gas_production Nm³/t FM Q_gas / Q_total specific_ch4_production Nm³/t FM Q_ch4 / Q_total HRT d V_liq divided by the volume flow the model uses for this feed

The units of Q_total and of the specific yields hold for the default Feedstock convention. The metrics contain no VFA, TAC or FOS/TAC values.

docs.text: The blocks below are the output of one run; ... marks omitted lines. The Total time lines are from that run on one PC and differ between machines and runs. The simulated values repeat from run to run, because the Monte Carlo draws are fixed by seed=42.

docs.title: Parameter Sweep
docs.text:
3. Parameter sweep over k_m_ac...  
   k_m_ac of the model at 42 °C: 11.76 1/d

docs.title: Adapting the Example
docs.text:
• Other parameters: every key of the table in step 2 can be used in a scenario, as parameter_name of a sweep or in parameter_distributions. nominal_rate returns the rate of the model for the k_dis_*, k_hyd_* and k_m_* keys.
  • Temperature: add T_ad in kelvin to a scenario, for example {"Q": base_feed, "T_ad": 311.15}. All scenarios of one call can have different temperatures.
  • Time series: pass save_time_series=True and a step dt in days to run_scenarios, parameter_sweep or monte_carlo. Each result then carries the last ten stored values of Q_gas, Q_ch4 and pH. Without save_time_series=True, dt has no effect.
  • Calibrated base model: parameters set with adm1.set_calibration_parameters({...}) on the base model apply to every scenario. A scenario value for the same parameter takes precedence.
  • Substrates and digester size: change the substrate list of Feedstock and the arguments of ADM1. The feed vectors follow the order of the substrate list.
  • Number of workers: set n_workers. Every call of run_scenarios starts its own pool. With n_workers=1 or a single scenario the simulator runs in the main process and starts no pool.
  • Failed scenarios: a scenario that raises an exception does not stop the others. Its result has success=False and the reason in error.

Several parameters can be varied at once with multi_parameter_sweep, which the script does not use. It simulates every combination of the given values:

results = parallel.multi_parameter_sweep(
    parameter_configs={"k_m_ac": [3.5, 8.0], "T_ad": [311.15, 315.15]},
    duration=duration,
    initial_state=initial_state,
    fixed_params={"Q": base_feed},
)

This gives 2 × 2 = 4 scenarios. In the result list the last parameter changes fastest: (3.5, 311.15), (3.5, 315.15), (8.0, 311.15), (8.0, 315.15).

In your own scripts, keep the call inside a main() function behind if __name__ == "__main__":, as the example does. The workers are started with the spawn method (forkserver on Linux), which imports the main module again in every worker; see the Python documentation on multiprocessing. The environment variable PYADM1_MP_START_METHOD selects another start method.

It saves one figure per study to output/.
  • Simulation API: Reference of ParallelSimulator, ScenarioResult, ParameterSweepConfig and MonteCarloConfig

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
1. One base model, many scenarios: ParallelSimulator sends the configuration of the base model to worker processes, and every scenario changes the feed, the temperature or calibration parameters on top of it.
  2. Three ways to build scenarios: an explicit list (run_scenarios), one parameter over several values (parameter_sweep) and random draws from normal distributions (monte_carlo).
  3. Results as numbers: every scenario returns its final state and metrics such as dry gas flows in Nm³/d, methane content and pH; summarize_results condenses them into statistics.

docs.title: Two-Stage Biogas Plant Example
docs.text:
The examples/02_two_stage_plant.py example builds a two-stage biogas plant: a hydrolysis pre-tank and a main fermenter in series, one CHP unit with a flare, and one heating system per stage. It simulates ten days and prints the final state of both tanks.

The Colab notebook builds the same plant with other component IDs and a shorter run (5 days in daily steps), so its numbers differ from the ones on this page.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The example shows:

  • Two ADM1 digesters in series, joined by a liquid connection
  • The gas storage that add_digester creates for each digester
  • One CHP unit fed from both gas storages, with its automatically created flare
  • One heating system per stage, tied to its digester and supplied with heat from the CHP
  • Saving the plant to a JSON file

docs.text:

The diagram shows the eight components and ten connections that the plant summary in the output below lists; the arrow labels are the connection types. A control connection hands the temperature and the feed of a digester to its heating system. The dashed arrows are not connections: the substrate feed is set as Q_substrates on the pre-tank, and the digestate is the effluent of the main fermenter. The flare is connected behind the CHP; it burns the gas that the gas storages vent.

docs.title: Digesters
docs.text:
Property Hydrolysis pre-tank Main fermenter Component ID hydrolysis main_digester Liquid volume V_liq 500 m³ 1000 m³ Gas headspace V_gas 75 m³ 150 m³ Temperature T_ad 318.15 K (45 °C) 308.15 K (35 °C) Substrate feed 11.4 t/d maize silage, 6.1 t/d swine manure None Inflow 16.2 m³/d of substrate 16.2 m³/d from the pre-tank Retention time 30.9 d 61.7 d

The feed rates are tonnes of fresh matter per day, 17.5 t/d in total. The feedstock converts them to a volume flow with the density of each substrate: 11.4 t/d of maize silage at 1129 kg/m³ are 10.1 m³/d, and swine manure counts with 1000 kg/m³. Together this gives 16.2 m³/d (see Volumetric ADM1da convention for Q). The retention time is the liquid volume divided by this flow. The script takes the flow from feedstock.actual_Q and prints the rounded retention times, 31 d and 62 d, in its start banner.

docs.title: Gas and Energy Components
docs.text:
Component ID Created by Settings Gas storage, pre-tank hydrolysis_storage add_digester Membrane storage, capacity 75 m³ Gas storage, main fermenter main_digester_storage add_digester Membrane storage, capacity 150 m³ CHP chp_1 add_chp 500 kW electrical (nominal), eta_el=0.40, eta_th=0.45 Flare chp_1_flare add_chp Destruction efficiency 0.98 Heating, pre-tank heating_hydro add_heating Target 318.15 K, tied to hydrolysis, 0.5 kW/K heat loss Heating, main fermenter heating_main add_heating Target 308.15 K, tied to main_digester, 0.5 kW/K heat loss

A digester holds no gas itself: V_gas is the headspace of the ADM1 gas phase, and the gas that leaves it goes into the separate GasStorage component <digester_id>_storage. The capacity of that storage is V_gas, but at least 50 m³. The destruction efficiency of the flare and the heat loss coefficient of 0.5 kW/K are package defaults; the script does not set them.

docs.title: Code Walkthrough
docs.text: The excerpts are taken from the script; most print calls are left out.

docs.title: 1. Feedstock and Feed Rates
docs.text:
feedstock = Feedstock(["maize_silage_milk_ripeness", "swine_manure"])

# Substrate feed in t FM/d, one slot per substrate of the feedstock:
# hydrolysis stage gets fresh substrate, main stage inherits.
hydro_feed = [11.4, 6.1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
main_feed = [0.0] * 10

# The model works with the volume flow of the feed [m³/d]: the feedstock
# converts the mass flows with the density of each substrate.
q_feed = sum(feedstock.actual_Q(hydro_feed))
  • The order of the substrate IDs defines the slots of the feed lists: slot 0 is maize silage (milk ripeness), slot 1 is swine manure, the other slots stay at zero. The bundled substrates are listed under Example Substrates.
  • The feed rates are tonnes of fresh matter per day.
  • main_feed holds only zeros: the main fermenter gets no substrate of its own, only the effluent of the pre-tank.
  • feedstock.actual_Q returns the volume flow of each substrate. Their sum q_feed is the 16.2 m³/d the model works with.

docs.title: 2. Two Digesters
docs.text:
plant = BiogasPlant("Two-Stage Plant (ADM1 / SIMBA# biogas)")
cfg = PlantConfigurator(plant, feedstock)

# Hydrolysis pre-tank — 45 °C, between the mesophilic and the thermophilic range
hydro_digester, _ = cfg.add_digester(
    digester_id="hydrolysis",
    V_liq=500.0,
    V_gas=75.0,
    T_ad=318.15,
    name="Hydrolysis Pre-Tank",
    Q_substrates=hydro_feed,
)
hrt_hydro = hydro_digester.V_liq / q_feed

# Main methanogenesis fermenter — larger volume, mesophilic.
# Its inflow is the effluent of the pre-tank, which has the same volume flow.
main_digester, _ = cfg.add_digester(
    digester_id="main_digester",
    V_liq=1000.0,
    V_gas=150.0,
    T_ad=308.15,
    name="Main Fermenter",
    Q_substrates=main_feed,
)
hrt_main = main_digester.V_liq / q_feed
  • Both stages use the same Digester class. There is no separate hydrolysis model; volume, temperature and feed decide what happens in a tank.
  • No initial-state file is needed: add_digester derives the initial state of each tank from the feedstock and the feed rates.
  • Each call also creates the gas storage <digester_id>_storage and connects the digester to it.
  • add_digester returns the digester. The script divides its liquid volume by q_feed to get the retention time for the start banner.

docs.title: 3. CHP, Flare and Heating
docs.text:
# CHP + heating. digester_id ties each heating system to its digester, so
# its heat demand covers the heat loss of the tank and warming the feed.
cfg.add_chp(chp_id="chp_1", P_el_nom=500.0, eta_el=0.40, eta_th=0.45)
cfg.add_heating(
    heating_id="heating_hydro",
    target_temperature=318.15,
    name="Hydrolysis Heating",
    digester_id="hydrolysis",
)
cfg.add_heating(
    heating_id="heating_main",
    target_temperature=308.15,
    name="Main Stage Heating",
    digester_id="main_digester",
)
  • add_chp also creates the flare chp_1_flare and connects it behind the CHP.
  • digester_id adds a control connection from the digester to the heating system. The heating system then receives the temperature and the substrate feed of the digester, and its heat demand is the heat loss plus the heat for warming the feed.
  • The digesters define no k-values, so the heat loss uses the default coefficient: 0.5 kW/K × (digester temperature − ambient temperature).
  • target_temperature of a heating system is not linked to T_ad of the digester; the script sets both to the same value.

docs.title: 4. Connections
docs.text:
cfg.connect("hydrolysis", "main_digester", "liquid")
cfg.auto_connect_digester_to_chp("hydrolysis", "chp_1")
cfg.auto_connect_digester_to_chp("main_digester", "chp_1")
cfg.auto_connect_chp_to_heating("chp_1", "heating_hydro")
cfg.auto_connect_chp_to_heating("chp_1", "heating_main")

plant.initialize()
print(plant.get_summary())
  • The liquid connection passes the effluent of the pre-tank, flow and composition, to the main fermenter.
  • auto_connect_digester_to_chp connects the gas storage of the digester to the CHP, not the digester itself.
  • auto_connect_chp_to_heating adds a heat connection. The heat of the CHP is split equally between the heating systems connected to it.

docs.title: 5. Simulation
docs.text:
duration = 10.0
dt = 1.0 / 24.0
results = plant.simulate(duration=duration, dt=dt, save_interval=1.0)

The run takes 240 steps of one hour. results holds eleven entries: one after the first step and one per full day. Each entry has the keys time and components; components maps every component ID to the outputs of that component.

docs.title: 6. Final State and JSON Export
docs.text:
final = results[-1]
h = final["components"]["hydrolysis"]
m = final["components"]["main_digester"]

total_gas = h["Q_gas"] + m["Q_gas"]
total_ch4 = h["Q_ch4"] + m["Q_ch4"]

The script prints Q_gas, Q_ch4, pH, VFA and TAC of both digesters and the sums of the two gas flows. It then saves the plant:

output_path = REPO_ROOT / "output"
output_path.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
plant.to_json(str(output_path / "two_stage_plant_config.json"))

BiogasPlant.from_json(path, feedstock) rebuilds the plant from this file. The feedstock has to be passed again because the file does not contain it.

docs.title: Gas Handling in One Plant Step
docs.text:
plant.simulate calls BiogasPlant.step() once per time step. A step runs every component once, in this order:

  1. The digesters: first the pre-tank, then the main fermenter with the effluent the pre-tank produced in the same step.
  2. The gas storages: each storage takes in the gas its digester produced in this step, supplies the CHP, and only then vents what exceeds its capacity to the flare.
  3. The CHP with the gas the storages supplied, then the heating systems with the heat of the CHP.
  4. The flare with the gas the storages vented.

The CHP asks for the gas it needs at full load and spreads this demand equally over the two storages. Because supply and venting are settled within the same step, the vented volume does not depend on the step length. See Gas Balance in a Plant.

docs.title: Final State on Day 10
docs.text:
Quantity Hydrolysis pre-tank Main fermenter Plant Biogas, dry [Nm³/d] 1679.0 216.6 1895.6 Methane [Nm³/d] 891.1 114.0 1005.1 Methane content of the dry gas 53.1 % 52.6 % 53.0 % Share of the plant's methane 88.7 % 11.3 % 100 % pH 7.42 7.39 – VFA [g HAc-eq/L] 0.24 0.03 – TAC [g CaCO3/L] 5.73 6.30 – VFA/TAC 0.04 0.005 –

Gas flows are dry gas at standard conditions. Q_gas and Q_ch4 are given in Nm³/d (0 °C, 1.01325 bar) and contain no water vapour. The methane content of 53.0 % is therefore that of the dry gas, which is what a gas analyser shows. See Reported gas flows.

The pre-tank produces most of the gas. 891.1 of the 1005.1 Nm³/d of methane (88.7 %) come from the first tank. With a retention time of 30.9 d, a pH of 7.42 and 0.24 g HAc-eq/L of VFA it runs the complete degradation chain down to methane. In this configuration it is not a separate acidification stage. The main fermenter digests what is left and adds 114.0 Nm³/d of methane.

Acids and buffer capacity. The VFA are 0.24 and 0.03 g HAc-eq/L at a TAC of 5.73 and 6.30 g CaCO3/L, which gives VFA/TAC ratios of 0.04 and 0.005. The pH is 7.42 and 7.39. Typical ranges of these indicators are listed under Optimal Operating Ranges.

Yield per tonne of feed. The 17.5 t/d of fresh matter give 108 Nm³ of biogas and 57 Nm³ of methane per tonne on day 10.

docs.title: Further Results
docs.text:
main() returns the plant and the result list. The outputs of the other components can be read from them, for example:

plant, results = main()
final = results[-1]["components"]

chp = final["chp_1"]
print(f"CHP electrical power:  {chp['P_el']:6.1f} kW")
print(f"CHP thermal power:     {chp['P_th']:6.1f} kW")
print(f"CHP gas consumption:   {chp['Q_gas_consumed']:6.1f} Nm³/d")

for storage_id in ("hydrolysis_storage", "main_digester_storage"):
    storage = final[storage_id]
    print(f"{storage_id}: {storage['stored_volume_m3']:.1f} m³ stored, {storage['cumulative_vented_m3']:.1f} m³ vented")
print(f"chp_1_flare: {final['chp_1_flare']['cumulative_vented_m3']:.1f} m³ burnt")

for heating_id in ("heating_hydro", "heating_main"):
    heating = final[heating_id]
    print(f"{heating_id}: {heating['Q_heat_supplied']:.1f} kW supplied, {heating['P_aux_heat']:.1f} kW auxiliary heat")

balance = plant.get_electricity_balance()
print(f"Net electrical power:  {balance['P_el_net']:6.1f} kW")

CHP electrical power:   167.5 kW
CHP thermal power:      188.4 kW
CHP gas consumption:   1895.6 Nm³/d
hydrolysis_storage: 0.0 m³ stored, 0.0 m³ vented
main_digester_storage: 0.0 m³ stored, 0.0 m³ vented
chp_1_flare: 0.0 m³ burnt
heating_hydro: 37.6 kW supplied, 0.0 kW auxiliary heat
heating_main: 10.0 kW supplied, 0.0 kW auxiliary heat
Net electrical power:   162.5 kW

The CHP runs at one third of its nominal power. 1005.1 Nm³/d of methane at 10 kWh/Nm³ are 418.8 kW of fuel power. With the electrical efficiency of 0.40 this gives 167.5 kW, 33.5 % of the nominal 500 kW. The thermal power is 167.5 kW × 0.45 / 0.40 = 188.4 kW. At full load the CHP would need 3000 Nm³/d of methane, about three times the production.

The storages stay empty and the flare is not used. The CHP can burn more gas than the digesters produce, so it takes all the gas of every step: its consumption of 1895.6 Nm³/d equals the production. Both storages are empty at the end of the step, and nothing is vented.

The heat demand is heat loss plus feed warming. The pre-tank needs 37.6 kW: 0.5 kW/K × (45 °C − 15 °C) = 15.0 kW of heat loss and 22.6 kW for warming the 17.5 t/d of feed to 45 °C. The substrates enter at their storage temperatures, 9.3 °C for the maize silage and 20 °C for the swine manure. The main fermenter needs 0.5 kW/K × (35 °C − 15 °C) = 10.0 kW. It has no substrate feed, and the inflow from the pre-tank is not part of the heat balance. 15 °C is the default ambient temperature of BiogasPlant. The 188.4 kW of CHP heat cover the 47.6 kW, so no auxiliary heat is needed.

Net power. The CHP uses 3 % of its output for its own auxiliaries (package default). The plant has no other electricity consumers, which leaves 162.5 kW.

The course over the ten days shows how far the plant is from a steady state:

for r in results:
    c = r["components"]
    q_gas = c["hydrolysis"]["Q_gas"] + c["main_digester"]["Q_gas"]
    q_ch4 = c["hydrolysis"]["Q_ch4"] + c["main_digester"]["Q_ch4"]
    print(
        f"{r['time']:5.2f} {c['hydrolysis']['Q_gas']:9.1f} {c['main_digester']['Q_gas']:8.1f}"
        f" {100 * q_ch4 / q_gas:6.1f} {c['chp_1']['P_el']:7.1f}"
    )

...

10.00    1679.0    216.6   53.0   167.5

The columns pre-tank and main are the biogas flows in Nm³/d. The first row is the state after the first hour: the tanks start from the derived initial state, the gas holds only 22.1 % methane, and the CHP also burns the initial filling of the storages (10 % of their capacity). From day 1 on the gas flow of the main fermenter rises from 104.2 to 216.6 Nm³/d and still gains 9.1 Nm³/d on the last day; the pre-tank gains 5.0 Nm³/d on that day. Ten days are a start-up phase at retention times of 30.9 and 61.7 d, so the final state above is not a steady state.

docs.title: Adapting the Example
docs.text:
• Feed: change the rates in hydro_feed (t/d of fresh matter) or pass other substrate IDs to Feedstock; see Example Substrates.
  • Stage sizes and temperatures: change V_liq, V_gas and T_ad in add_digester. A smaller V_liq of the pre-tank shortens its retention time. Set target_temperature of the matching heating system to the new T_ad.
  • Simulation length: change duration in plant.simulate to follow the plant beyond the start-up phase.
  • CHP: change P_el_nom, eta_el and eta_th in add_chp.
  • Heat demand: set heat_loss_coefficient in add_heating, or give the digesters the k-values k_wall, k_roof and k_ground in add_digester so that the heat loss follows the tank surfaces. The ambient temperature is T_ambient of BiogasPlant. See Heating System.
  • More components: mixers, substrate storages and feeders are added with add_mixer, add_substrate_storage and add_feeder; see Mechanical Components and Feeding Components.
  • Many scenarios: see Parallel Simulation.
