docs.title: Substrates
docs.text:
A substrate in PyADM1ODE is a file of laboratory values: dry matter, feed analysis, methane potential and the state in which the material reaches the digester. From these values the model computes the digester influent – how much degradable material arrives, how fast it degrades, and how much nitrogen and buffer it brings along.

from pyadm1 import Feedstock

# Two substrates of the library, chosen by file name without extension
feedstock = Feedstock(["maize_silage_milk_ripeness", "cattle_manure"])

The files live under data/substrates/. The amount of each substrate (Q_substrates, in tonnes of fresh matter per day) is set at the digester, in the order of the list above.

docs.title: What this section answers
docs.text:
Question Page Which example substrates exist, and which one suits what? Example substrates What do the values of a substrate file mean, and which ranges are realistic? Parameters & ranges What changes in the simulation when a value is different? Influence of the values Where do the values of the bundled files come from? Origin of the values

Reference values – define your own substrates for real plants

The bundled substrates describe typical material, not the substrate of a particular plant. They are suitable for demos, tests and studies, but are no substitute for measured data. To model a real plant, characterise your own substrate (TS / VS, Weender and cell-wall analysis, BMP from a batch test) and add a new file under data/substrates/. The page Parameters & ranges shows which values that takes.

docs.title: Your own substrate in three steps
docs.text:
1. Copy the library file of the most similar material, for example maize_silage_milk_ripeness.yaml to my_maize.yaml.
  2. Enter your own laboratory values. Required are TS, VS, RP, RL, pH and one of the three values BMP, D_VS or aXI; everything else is optional.
  3. Load the file by its name or its path: 
from pyadm1 import Feedstock
from pyadm1.substrates import load_substrate

feedstock = Feedstock(["my_maize", "cattle_manure"])       # lives in data/substrates/
my_maize = load_substrate("path/to/my_maize.yaml")          # or by path

A misspelt parameter name raises an error; it is not silently skipped.

How the file becomes the 38-column ADM1 influent stream is described on the page ADM1 implementation.

docs.title: Influence of the Values
docs.text: Every value of a substrate file acts on one of four quantities of the simulation: how much gas forms, how fast it forms, how much nitrogen reaches the digester, and how well the digester is buffered. This page first shows which value acts on what, then a worked example with numbers, and finally the formulas behind it.

docs.title: Which value acts on what
docs.text: Value Acts on Direction TS Gas amount, nitrogen load, loading rate More dry matter per tonne brings proportionally more of everything: gas, nitrogen, organic load. VS Gas amount More organic matter in the dry matter, correspondingly less ash. BMP (or D_VS, aXI) Gas amount Sets which share of the organic matter is degradable. The rest leaves the digester as inert material. NDF Speed More cell wall moves degradable material from the fast to the slow pool. At a fixed BMP the potential stays the same, but in the digester a larger part is washed out before it is degraded. ADL Almost nothing while BMP is given Lignin is inert. At a fixed BMP the degradation level is fitted so that the potential matches; ADL then only shifts the make-up of the inert rest. With a fixed D_VS, ADL limits how much of the cell wall is degradable. RP Nitrogen, pH, inhibition Protein releases ammonium when degraded. More protein raises ammonium and pH and can inhibit methane formation. RL Methane content Lipids yield more methane per kilogram and a gas richer in methane than carbohydrates. NDICP Speed of protein degradation Protein bound in the cell wall is only released with the cell wall and goes to the slow pool. NH4 / Snh4 Nitrogen, pH, inhibition Ammonium the substrate already carries. Acts like RP, but at once. KS43 / TAC Buffer Bicarbonate of the substrate. Together with ammonium and acids it sets the charge balance of the influent. Sac, Spro, Sbu, Sva (or FFS) Acid load Acids already fermented. They are available at once and burden the buffer; propionate and butyrate first have to be converted to acetate. pH Charge balance of the influent Sets which share of the acids and the ammonium is dissociated, and with it the cations and anions the substrate brings along. Temp Heat demand No influence on the biology (the digester has its own temperature), but on the heating: every kelvin colder costs about 1.2 kWh of heat per tonne of substrate. cost Costs Only enters the cost calculation. substrate_class Defaults A slurry or manure class assigns protein and lipids without a measurement to the slow pool, otherwise to the fast one.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
A digester of 3000 m³ at 40 °C receives 30 t of maize silage (maize_silage_milk_ripeness) and 10 t of cattle slurry (cattle_manure) per day, with the default kinetics. In each row one value of one file is changed, everything else stays the same. Shown is the steady state after 400 days. The half-time is the time after which the methane production has reached half of its rise when the maize amount steps up by 50 %.

Changed value Methane [Nm³/d] Change VFA [g/l] pH NH₄-N [g/l] Half-time [d] Base case 2731 – 0.6 7.45 2.20 5.0 Maize TS 28 instead of 32.6 % 2361 −14 % 0.2 7.42 1.97 4.3 Maize TS 38 % 3155 +15 % 2.3 7.43 2.51 5.6 Maize VS 92 instead of 94 % 2669 −2 % 0.7 7.45 2.23 5.2 Maize VS 96 % 2794 +2 % 0.5 7.45 2.18 4.8 Maize BMP 300 instead of 338 2460 −10 % 1.0 7.45 2.30 5.0 Maize BMP 370 2959 +8 % 0.4 7.44 2.12 4.9 Maize NDF 40 instead of 54.6 % 2817 +3 % 0.5 7.45 2.17 4.1 Maize NDF 65 % 2670 −2 % 0.7 7.45 2.23 6.0 Maize ADL 2 or 7 instead of 4.6 % 2731 0 % 0.6 7.45 2.20 5.0 Maize RP 5 instead of 6.4 % 2736 0 % 0.1 7.36 1.65 4.2 Maize RP 10 % 2610 −4 % 10.7 7.22 3.65 5.7 Maize RL 2 instead of 3 % 2721 0 % 0.6 7.45 2.20 5.0 Maize RL 5 % 2752 +1 % 0.7 7.46 2.21 4.9 Maize Sac 1 instead of 4.2 g/l 2725 0 % 0.5 7.44 2.19 4.9 Maize Sac 10 g/l 2741 0 % 0.9 7.47 2.22 5.1 Maize pH 3.6 or 4.3 instead of 3.9 2732 / 2729 0 % 0.5 / 0.8 7.45 / 7.47 2.20 4.9 / 5.2 Slurry TS 5 instead of 10 % 2666 −2 % 0.4 7.44 2.11 4.7 Slurry BMP 150 instead of 212 2693 −1 % 0.5 7.45 2.15 4.8 Slurry NH4 1.5 instead of 2.4 kg N/m³ 2735 0 % 0.3 7.47 1.92 4.5 Slurry NH4 4.5 kg N/m³ 2711 −1 % 2.2 7.37 2.85 5.6 Slurry KS43 50 instead of 109 mol/m³ 2735 0 % 0.4 7.41 2.21 4.6 Slurry KS43 250 mol/m³ 2710 −1 % 2.2 7.49 2.20 5.8 Slurry Temp 5 or 20 instead of 10 °C 2731 0 % 0.6 7.45 2.20 5.0

What the table shows:

  • The gas amount hangs on TS and BMP. Both act almost proportionally. They are the values to measure first for a real plant.
  • NDF sets the sluggishness. Between 40 and 65 % cell wall the half-time lies between 4.1 and 6.0 days; the gas amount changes by a few percent only.
  • Nitrogen decides on stability. More protein or ammonium raises the ammonium in the digester, and the acids rise. At 10 % crude protein in the maize the digester tips over (11 g/l acids).
  • The storage state of the silage is secondary. pH and acetic acid of the silage change the gas amount by less than 0.5 %.
  • More buffer in the substrate does not help here. More bicarbonate in the slurry raises the pH, with it the share of free ammonia, and the acids rise. This holds only because the base case already sits close to ammonia inhibition.

The model is sensitive to nitrogen

With the default kinetics the base case already sits close to ammonia inhibition. Protein-rich rations (grass silage, poultry manure, much slurry) lead to high acid levels faster in the model than in practice, where the biology adapts to ammonia. If you compute such rations, calibrate the inhibition constant K_I_nh3 against plant data.

The numbers hold for this one operating point. At another loading rate or retention time the magnitudes change, the directions remain.

docs.title: How the measured values are used
docs.text:
Cell wall instead of crude fibre. With NDF and ADL the carbohydrates are split by the cell wall:

slow pool   X_PS_ch = d · (NDF − ADL)                 structural carbohydrates
fast pool   X_PF_ch = VS − RP − RL − NDF              non-fibre carbohydrates
inert       X_I     = ADL + (1 − d) · (NDF − ADL)     lignin and non-degradable fibre
            d       = (NDF − VS · (1 − D_VS)) / (NDF − ADL)

The non-degradable volatile solids VS · (1 − D_VS) are assigned to the cell wall, lignin first (Koch et al. 2010). Protein and lipids count as degradable. d is limited to 0…1: non-degradable matter beyond the whole cell wall is spread over the cell contents, and lignin stays inert even if D_VS claims more. Each fraction is converted to COD with its own factor, lignin with 1.563 kgCOD/kg. The total COD equals the COD of the composition, and the degraded share of the volatile solids equals D_VS.

Inert share from a measured methane potential. With BMP and neither D_VS nor aXI, the degradability is fitted until the model potential equals the measured one:

model potential = degradable COD · 0.350 Nm³ CH4/kgCOD / VS  =  BMP / BMP_recovery

With a cell-wall analysis the degradation level D_VS is fitted, otherwise the inert share aXI. Both change the potential monotonically, so the result is unique. A potential the composition cannot reach raises an error. The same applies to a file of the standard schema that gives BMP but no aXI; in code, fit_degradability_to_bmp(params) does the fit.

BMP_recovery defaults to 1: the model potential is matched to the measured one directly. Two effects of opposite sign are left out by that. A batch test recovers about 5 % less methane than the degradable COD holds, because biomass grows (Weißbach 2009). The model counts carbohydrates as glucose, which is about 10 % below the COD of starch and cellulose. Setting BMP_recovery: 0.95 accounts for the first effect alone; for the cereal whole-plant silage and the onions the composition then no longer reaches the standard yield.

Protein bound in the cell wall. NDICP (neutral detergent insoluble crude protein, Licitra et al. 1996) is the protein that stays in the NDF residue. It is released only as the cell wall disintegrates and enters the slow pool; the remaining protein enters the fast pool:

slow pool   X_PS_pr = NDICP                     X_PS_ch = d · (NDF − NDICP − ADL)
fast pool   X_PF_pr = RP − NDICP                X_PF_ch = VS − RP − RL − (NDF − NDICP)

The bound protein is weighed with the NDF, so it is taken out of the structural carbohydrates; this is the non-fibre carbohydrate formula of NRC (2001). fsOTS / ffOTS then only split the lipids. Lipids have no such measurement: the detergent removes them, they belong to the cell contents.

Single acids. Each acid enters its own ADM1 state. Propionate and butyrate then pass acetogenesis, which FFS (all acetate) skips.

Titrated acid capacity. A titration to pH 4.3 also protonates acid anions. They are subtracted, so only the rest counts as bicarbonate:

S_hco3 = TAC − Σ S_acid · (α(pH) − α(4.3))        limited to ≥ 0

For the swine manure of the Gummersbach plant this leaves 51 instead of 212 mol/m³. KS43 of the standard schema is still taken as bicarbonate directly.

Filtrate COD. COD_S beyond the acids and the soluble inerts is matter that is already disintegrated. It enters the hydrolysable pools X_S_* and is taken out of the disintegration pools in proportion.

Biomass. X_bac and X_meth are split over the seven ADM1 groups in the ratios of the digester inoculum and taken out of the disintegration pools. load_gummersbach_library() adds the biomass of the legacy model to manure classes (0.25 and 0.0003 kgCOD/m³ at a storage age of 10 days); manure_age=None switches it off.

Remuneration class. substrate_class is free text and is not used by the model. The library uses the classes of the German EEG 2012 as listed in the BiomasseV: EK I for energy crops (Anlage 2), EK II for manure (Anlage 3), EK 0 for substrates without a substrate-related tariff (Anlage 1). A financial module can key tariffs, the maize cap or greenhouse-gas factors to it. The field is available in both schemas and is stored in SubstrateParams.

docs.title: What is still not measured
docs.text:
• The split of the lipids between the slow and the fast pool, and of the protein without NDICP (fsOTS / ffOTS). Default: slow for manure classes, fast otherwise. In the library only maize silage and corn-cob mix carry an NDICP; no sourced value was found for the other substrates.
  • The disintegration rates. The legacy library holds a rate kdis per substrate; ADM1da has two pools with fixed rates that are calibrated per digester. kdis, khyd_* and km_* are read and ignored.

docs.title: Differences to the legacy model
docs.text:
• One disintegration pool with a rate per substrate becomes two pools, split by the cell wall.
  • The legacy model subtracts all acid anions from TAC, not only the titrated share.
  • Density uses additive volumes instead of the mass-weighted mean.
  • cost of the legacy library is in EUR/m³ and is converted to EUR/t FM.

Quality of the legacy values

Several values of the legacy library are not measurements of the substrate they describe. NDF / ADF / ADL of maize are literature values; green rye, onions, corn-cob mix and solid cattle manure carry the same NDF without a source. The degradation level of swine manure (0.95) has no source. COD_S is labelled as an assumption for five substrates and has no source for the other four. The library files under data/substrates/ no longer use these values; gummersbach:<id> still does.

docs.title: Example Substrates
docs.text:
PyADM1ODE ships 13 substrate files under data/substrates/. Each describes typical material of one substrate type and is chosen by its file name without extension:

from pyadm1 import Feedstock
from pyadm1.substrates import SubstrateRegistry

SubstrateRegistry().available()      # all IDs of the library
feedstock = Feedstock(["maize_silage_milk_ripeness", "cattle_manure"])

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Feedstock() without arguments loads all 13 substrates in the order of the table; Q idx is then the position in the Q_substrates array.

Q idx Substrate ID Remuneration class TS [% FM] VS [% TS] BMP [Nm³ CH₄/t VS] CH₄ [m³/t FM] Degradable VS Slow pool [%] Carbohydrate split 0 maize_silage_milk_ripeness Mais (GPS) (EK I) 32.6 94.0 338 104 0.82 46 cell wall 1 cattle_manure Rindergülle (EK II) 10.0 84.1 212 18 0.49 100 crude fibre 2 swine_manure Schweinegülle (EK II) 7.9 84.8 250 17 0.51 100 crude fibre 3 corn_cob_mix Corn-Cob-Mix (CCM) (EK I) 65.0 98.5 380 243 0.93 9 cell wall 4 grass_silage Gras/Ackergras (EK I) 35.0 90.5 317 100 0.69 29 cell wall 5 green_rye_silage Grünroggen (GPS) (EK I) 25.0 90.5 320 72 0.77 38 cell wall 6 cereal_gps_silage Getreide (GPS) (EK I) 36.8 93.3 329 113 0.85 49 cell wall 7 onion_waste Gemüse (aussortiert) (EK 0) 10.9 96.8 379 40 0.96 12 cell wall 8 maize_silage_gummersbach Mais (GPS) (EK I) 32.0 96.2 338 104 0.82 30 cell wall 9 cattle_manure_solid Rinderfestmist (EK II) 25.0 84.1 249 52 0.68 100 crude fibre 10 chicken_manure_dry Geflügelmist, Geflügeltrockenkot (EK II) 45.0 78.0 273 96 0.59 87 cell wall 11 swine_manure_gummersbach Schweinegülle (EK II) 6.1 71.6 250 11 0.32 100 crude fibre 12 wheat_whole_plant_silage Getreide (GPS) (EK I) 36.8 93.3 329 113 0.84 47 cell wall

How to read the columns:

  • TS, VS, BMP are stated in the file. CH₄ [m³/t FM] is computed from them: the methane one tonne of fresh matter yields when fully degraded.
  • Degradable VS is the share of the volatile solids the model can degrade. It is the degradation level D_VS (cell-wall route) or the degradable share of the organic COD 1 − aXI − aSi (crude-fibre route).
  • Slow pool is the share of the degradable particulate material that disintegrates slowly. The higher it is, the more sluggishly the gas production follows a change in feeding.
  • Carbohydrate split names the fibre analysis the file uses: the cell wall after van Soest (NDF, ADL) or the crude fibre after Weender (RF).

docs.title: Energy crops (EK I)
docs.text: File Material Note maize_silage_milk_ripeness Maize silage, harvested early (milk ripeness) Much cell wall (55 % of TS), little starch. Today's dough-ripe silage holds about 40 % cell wall and degrades faster. maize_silage_gummersbach Maize silage of the Gummersbach plant Laboratory values of a real plant; goes with swine_manure_gummersbach. grass_silage Grass silage, meadow and ley grass Rich in protein; brings much nitrogen into the digester. green_rye_silage Green rye whole-plant silage The weakest file: composition taken from grass, fermentation quality from abroad. cereal_gps_silage, wheat_whole_plant_silage Whole-crop cereal silage Same composition (wheat); they differ only in lipids and price. corn_cob_mix Corn-cob-mix (CCM) Most energy-dense substrate, almost all of it fast degradable. The blend of 90 % grain and 10 % cob is an assumption.

docs.title: Manures (EK II)
docs.text: File Material Note cattle_manure Cattle slurry, 10 % TS Little gas per tonne, but buffer and ammonium. swine_manure Pig slurry, 8 % TS More ammonium than cattle slurry. swine_manure_gummersbach Pig slurry of the Gummersbach plant Thinner (6 % TS) and high in ash. cattle_manure_solid Solid cattle manure, 25 % TS Stackable; the buffer is given as titrated acid capacity. chicken_manure_dry Dry poultry manure, 45 % TS Very rich in nitrogen; the protein includes the uric acid.

docs.title: Residues (EK 0)
docs.text:
File Material Note onion_waste Rejected onions Almost fully and quickly degradable, no ammonium, no buffer.

The sources behind the values of each file are listed on the page Origin of the values.

docs.title: Format examples
docs.text: data/substrates/examples/ holds the same substrate (cattle_manure) as YAML, XML and TOML, plus maize_silage_measured.yaml as a template for a file of measured values. These files are not part of the library and are loaded by path.

docs.title: Legacy Gummersbach library
docs.text:
The substrate library of the predecessor model with ten substrates (ccm, cowmanure, futterkalk, gps, grass, greenrye, maize, onions, swinemanure, wheat) is included as one XML file and chosen with the prefix gummersbach::

from pyadm1 import Feedstock
from pyadm1.substrates import load_gummersbach_library

library = load_gummersbach_library()
feedstock = Feedstock(["gummersbach:maize", "gummersbach:swinemanure"])

Several of its values are not measurements of the substrate described; see Differences to the legacy model.

docs.title: Superseded files
docs.text:
The files the library held before are kept in data/substrates/legacy/. They are not part of the registry and are selected by the prefix legacy::

from pyadm1 import Feedstock

old = Feedstock(["legacy:maize_silage_milk_ripeness", "legacy:cattle_manure"])

Results obtained with an earlier version are reproduced this way. The most visible changes of the new files: cattle and pig slurry hold 45 to 65 % more degradable COD (the superseded ifak values lie well below the KTBL yields), maize silage puts 46 instead of 23 % of its degradable COD into the slow pool, and the bicarbonate of the Gummersbach pig slurry drops from 212 to 51 mol/m³ because its acid capacity is now read as a titration value.

docs.title: Parameters & Ranges
docs.text: A substrate file holds four groups of values. This page explains what each value means, how it is measured, and in which range it usually lies for agricultural substrates. What a change does in the simulation is covered on the page Influence of the values.

docs.title: Dry matter and composition
docs.text:
Value Unit Meaning Measurement TS % of fresh matter Total solids: what remains after drying at 105 °C. The rest is water. Drying oven VS % of TS Volatile solids: the part of the TS that burns at 550 °C. The rest is ash. Loss on ignition RP % of TS Crude protein: nitrogen × 6.25. Kjeldahl RL % of TS Crude lipids. Ether extraction RF % of TS Crude fibre after Weender. Only needed when NDF and ADL are missing. Weender analysis NDF % of TS Neutral detergent fibre: the whole cell wall (cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin). van Soest ADF % of TS Acid detergent fibre: cellulose and lignin. Stored, but not used. van Soest ADL % of TS Acid detergent lignin: the non-degradable part of the cell wall. van Soest NDICP % of TS Protein bound in the cell wall. Needs NDF and ADL. Nitrogen in the NDF residue

What remains of the volatile solids after protein, lipids and fibre is counted by the model as easily degradable carbohydrates (starch, sugars).

docs.title: Degradability
docs.text:
At least one of these three values must be given. If several are given, the order of precedence is D_VS, aXI, BMP.

Value Unit Meaning Measurement BMP Nm³ CH₄ per t VS Methane potential: the methane formed on complete degradation. The model fits the degradable share so that its potential equals this value. Batch digestion test (VDI 4630) D_VS 0…1 Degradation level: the share of the VS that is degradable. Digestibility, digestion test aXI 0…1 Inert share of the particulate COD (standard schema). Not directly measurable BMP_recovery 0…1 Share of the degradable COD the digestion test recovers as methane. Default 1. –

docs.title: Storage state
docs.text:
The state of the substrate as it reaches the digester.

Value Unit Meaning pH – pH of the substrate. NH4 kg N/m³ Ammonium nitrogen. Alternatively Snh4 in g NH₄/l. Sac, Spro, Sbu, Sva g/l Acetic, propionic, butyric and valeric acid. Alternatively FFS as their sum in acetic acid equivalents. KS43 mol/m³ Bicarbonate. TAC mmol/l Titrated acid capacity to pH 4.3. Unlike KS43 it includes the acid anions titrated along; the loader subtracts them. Temp °C Temperature of the substrate in storage.

Lactic acid, the main fermentation acid of a silage, has no state of its own in the model. It is not entered; its energy stays in the carbohydrates.

docs.title: Other
docs.text: Value Unit Meaning cost EUR per t fresh matter Price free plant; see Substrate costs. substrate_class Text Remuneration class, for example "Rindergülle (EK II)". A slurry or manure class selects the defaults for manures. COD_S, SIin g COD/l COD of the filtrate and soluble inert COD. Optional. X_bac, X_meth kg COD/m³ Living biomass in the substrate (slurry, manure). Optional.

docs.title: Realistic ranges
docs.text:
The ranges below come from published reference tables and serve to check your own values for plausibility. They are spans over many farms and harvest years; a value outside is not wrong, but it should have a reason.

The loader checks consistency, not plausibility

A substrate file with values outside the ranges below loads without a message. The loader rejects only what cannot be right: a misspelt parameter name, TS or VS outside 0–100, a pH outside 0–14, negative concentrations, RP + RL + NDF above VS, and detergent fibres that are not nested (ADL ≤ ADF ≤ NDF). One thing stays yours to watch: all contents are given in percent, not as a fraction (32.6, not 0.326).

docs.title: Dry matter, organic matter, methane yield
docs.text:
Range and, in brackets, mean after the Leitfaden Biogas (FNR 2016, tables 4.1–4.4 and 4.9). The guide does not list CCM and onions; their values are single values of the database "Biogasausbeute" of LfL Bavaria, where the methane yield is computed from biogas yield and methane content.

Smallest and largest value of the Feedipedia datasheets (INRAE, CIRAD, AFZ, FAO), in percent of dry matter. For green rye silage the table values of the Gruber Tabelle (LfL 2024) from ear emergence to after flowering.

Substrate RP RL RF NDF ADF ADL Ash (100 − VS) Maize silage, 30–35 % TS 4.7–9.3 1.3–4.0 15–26 38–55 19–33 1.9–5.1 2.1–5.4 Maize silage, 25–30 % TS 4.9–9.8 1.0–3.9 17–27 38–63 21–35 2.0–7.0 2.3–5.7 Whole-crop cereal silage (barley) 6.6–12.4 1.7–3.1 32–35 38–56 23–36 2.5–7.1 4.7–17.3 Grass silage (timothy) 9.4–17.2 – 28–35 47–64 28–42 3.6–3.8 5.7–11.2 Green rye silage 12–15 3.7–4.5 26–34 53–65 31–38 – – Ear maize silage (closest to CCM) 7.5–10.9 3.7–4.5 2.8–7.9 12–25 4.5–12 1.3–2.0 1.6–3.0

With rising maturity the cell wall of maize falls and the starch rises: starch lies between 11 and 37 % of dry matter at 25–30 % TS, and between 21 and 42 % at 35–40 % TS. The library file maize_silage_milk_ripeness sits at the upper edge with 54.6 % NDF.

docs.title: Fermentation quality of silages
docs.text:
Typical ranges of well-fermented silages after Kung & Shaver (2001), in percent of dry matter.

Value Maize silage (30–40 % TS) Grass silage (30–35 % TS) pH 3.7–4.2 4.3–4.7 Lactic acid 4–7 6–10 Acetic acid 1–3 1–3 Propionic acid < 0.1 < 0.1 Butyric acid 0 0.5–1.0 Ammonia N [% of crude protein] 5–7 8–12

The file expects acids in g/l of fresh matter. The conversion:

acid [g/l] ≈ acid [% of TS] · TS [% FM] / 10

So 1–3 % acetic acid in a maize silage of 33 % TS are 3.3–10 g/l (Sac). More than 0.5 % butyric acid indicates a faulty fermentation.

docs.title: Storage state of slurry and manure
docs.text:
Value Cattle slurry Pig slurry Source pH 6.3–7.9 (7.3) 6.5–7.9 (7.1) Pizzul et al. 2018 Ammonium nitrogen [kg/t] 0.6–2.7 (2.0) 1.5–5.2 (2.8) Pizzul et al. 2018 Total nitrogen [kg/t] 1.5–5.1 (3.9) 1.7–8.9 (4.6) Pizzul et al. 2018 NH4 after fertiliser reference value [kg N/m³] 1.6–2.1 3.0–3.4 (finishing), 2.3–2.8 (sows) LfL Basisdaten 2024

For solid manure the LfL fertiliser reference values give 0.4 kg NH₄-N per tonne (cattle manure, 18.5–23 % TS) and 7–9 kg per tonne (chicken manure and droppings, 52–59 % TS). These values hold at the time of spreading, after housing and storage losses.

For the acid capacity (KS43, TAC) and the fatty acids of raw slurry no source with a range was found. The library values (bicarbonate 109–112 mol/m³, fatty acids 8–10 g/l) rest on one fresh sample each; see Origin of the values.

docs.title: Measured parameters
docs.text:
The COD fractionation above (aXI, fOTSrf, fsOTS, ffOTS, aSi) follows SIMBA and cannot be measured directly. A substrate can instead be described by laboratory values. The library files are written this way; the names and units are those of the legacy Gummersbach substrate library.

from pyadm1 import Feedstock
from pyadm1.substrates import load_gummersbach_library, load_substrate

library = load_gummersbach_library()                    # bundled legacy library, 10 substrates
feedstock = Feedstock(["gummersbach:maize", "gummersbach:swinemanure"])   # by ID
maize = load_substrate("data/substrates/examples/maize_silage_measured.yaml")

A substrate file selects the schema with schema: measured (YAML, TOML) or <substrate schema="measured"> (XML). The older spelling schema: gummersbach is still accepted.

name: Maize silage (measured parameters)
schema: measured
substrate_class: "Mais (GPS) (EK I)"
TS:   31.97    # % FM
VS:   96.25    # % TS
RP:    8.69    # % TS
RL:    3.68    # % TS
NDF:  43.64    # % TS
ADL:   2.15    # % TS
NDICP: 1.3     # % TS
BMP:  338      # Nm³ CH4/t VS, sets the inert share
pH:    3.93
Sac:   1.18    # g/l
Snh4:  0.66    # g/l
TAC:   6.0     # mmol/l
Parameter Unit Meaning Replaces TS, VS % FM, % TS Total and volatile solids TS [kg/t], fRA RF, RP, RL % TS Weender analysis; RF is optional with NDF and ADL fRF, fRP, fRFe NDF, ADL % TS Cell wall and lignin after van Soest fOTSrf, fsOTS / ffOTS for carbohydrates ADF % TS Acid detergent fibre; stored, not used — NDICP % TS Protein bound in the cell wall; needs NDF and ADL fsOTS / ffOTS for protein D_VS – Degradation level of the volatile solids aXI, aSi BMP Nm³ CH₄/t VS Methane potential of a batch test; used without D_VS and aXI aXI or D_VS BMP_recovery – Share of the degradable COD the batch test recovers as methane, default 1 — Sac, Spro, Sbu, Sva g/l Single volatile fatty acids FFS TAC mmol/l Titrated acid capacity to pH 4.3 KS43 Snh4 g/l Ammonium, as NH₄ NH4 [kg N/m³] T °C Storage temperature Temp COD_S gCOD/l COD of the filtrate — SIin gCOD/l Soluble inert COD aSi X_bac, X_meth kgCOD/m³ Living bacteria and methanogens (manure) — substrate_class text Remuneration class; a manure class selects the manure defaults —

TS, VS, RP, RL and pH are required; everything else is optional. The inert share comes from D_VS, else from aXI, else from BMP; one of the three has to be given. A misspelled parameter name raises an error. The keys of the standard schema (NH4, KS43, FFS, Temp, fOTSrf, aSi, cost) are accepted too, in their own units.

docs.title: Substrate characterisation
docs.text:
The standard schema, after SIMBA, describes a substrate by this parameter set. The library files use the measured parameters instead, from which the same set is derived:

  • Proximate analysis — TS, NH4, biogas / biomethane potentials BGP, BMP.
  • Weender analysis — crude-fibre, crude-protein, crude-lipid, ash fractions of TS (fRF, fRP, fRFe, fRA).
  • COD fractionation — particulate-inert and dissolved-inert COD shares (aXI, aSi), biodegradable share of crude fibre (fOTSrf), slow / fast disintegration-pool split (fsOTS, ffOTS).
  • Physical / chemical state — substrate temperature, pH, acid capacity to pH 4.3 (KS43), VFAs as acetic-acid equivalent (FFS).

Component densities, mass-to-COD conversion factors, methane potentials, and the acid-base equilibrium constants are inherited from the model defaults in SubstrateParams and need only be specified per substrate when a measurement justifies overriding them.

See the ADM1 Implementation page for how the characterisation is turned into the 38-column ADM1 inflow stream.

docs.title: File formats
docs.text:
Each substrate can be defined as YAML (canonical), XML, or TOML. The loader dispatches on the file extension and produces the same SubstrateParams object in every case; see data/substrates/examples/ for side-by-side examples of the same substrate in all three formats.

from pyadm1.substrates import SubstrateRegistry, load_substrate

# By ID — discovers any supported format in data/substrates/
reg = SubstrateRegistry()
maize = reg.get("maize_silage_milk_ripeness")

# By explicit path — extension picks the loader
swine = load_substrate("data/substrates/swine_manure.yaml")

docs.title: Substrate costs
docs.text:
Each substrate may carry a cost in EUR per tonne of fresh matter, free plant. It is optional and defaults to 0. Set it in the substrate file or per feedstock:

# YAML
cost: 40.0      # EUR/t FM

# TOML
cost = 40.0     # EUR/t FM

<!-- XML -->
<param name="cost" value="40.0" unit="EUR/t_FM" description="Price free plant"/>

All substrates of the library carry an indicative price free plant (German market, 2022–2025). Energy crops are priced at roughly 105–125 EUR per tonne of dry matter, so their fresh-matter price follows the TS content; slurry carries transport only.

Substrate cost [EUR/t FM] Maize silage 40 Cereal / wheat whole-plant silage 36 / 35 Grass silage 33 Green rye silage 22 Corn-cob mix (CCM) 125 Chicken manure, dry 30 Cattle manure, solid 8 Onion waste 5 Cattle / swine manure (slurry) 2

The regional and yearly spread is large (silage maize alone 30–50 EUR/t FM); replace the value with the contract price of the plant.

feedstock.set_substrate_costs({"maize_silage_milk_ripeness": 40.0, "swine_manure": 2.0})
feedstock.substrate_costs        # {'maize_silage_milk_ripeness': 40.0, 'swine_manure': 2.0}

There are two ways to get the costs of an operation.

From any feed record — configured rates, a feed log, a flow sensor or an estimate. Pass one set of rates held for dt days, or a time series with one row per interval:

feedstock.calc_substrate_costs([10, 5], dt=30.0)          # 30 days at constant rates
feedstock.calc_substrate_costs(measured_feed, dt=1 / 24)  # hourly sensor readings
# {'total': 12300.0, 'by_substrate': {...}, 'mass_t': {...}}

From the simulation — the plant accumulates, on every step, what its digesters really received. With a feeder that is the dosed flow (including an empty storage or a blockage), not the configured rate:

plant.simulate(duration=90)
plant.get_substrate_costs()
# {'total': ..., 'by_substrate': {...}, 'mass_t': {...}, 'specific_cost': ...}  # EUR/t FM

Comparing the two shows how far the recorded feed deviates from the simulated one. The rates are in the unit of Q_substrates — tonnes per day with the default simba_q_convention=True, m³/d otherwise (converted through the substrate density).

docs.title: Origin of the Values
docs.text:
This page documents where the values of the 13 library files come from and where their limits lie.

Every value in a library file names its source in a comment. Five sources are combined, because no single one covers a substrate completely:

Source Supplies Parameters Phyllis database (TNO) Composition of the dry matter, as the median of a documented selection of samples VS, RP, RL, NDF, ADF, ADL; TS where the samples were analysed fresh BiomasseV 2012, Anlagen 1–3 Standard methane yield per tonne of fresh matter, converted with the KTBL standard dry matter BMP, substrate_class; TS where Phyllis has no fresh sample Published analyses of the material as it is fed (see Storage state) Storage state pH, ammonium, acids, bicarbonate or acid capacity, temperature Literature Protein bound in the cell wall NDICP of maize silage and corn-cob mix Superseded files; laboratory of the Gummersbach plant for its two files Price; storage state of the plant files cost; pH, acids, acid capacity of maize_silage_gummersbach and swine_manure_gummersbach

Phyllis is a database for thermochemical conversion. It holds ash, elemental and cell-wall analyses, but no pH, ammonium, fatty acids, acid capacity or methane potential; its only pH values belong to biochar and wood ash. These parameters cannot come from it.

docs.title: Phyllis samples
docs.text:
Material Samples Used for Maize, whole plant, five hybrids, analysed fresh, van Soest fibre #2603–#2607 TS, VS, cell wall of maize_silage_milk_ripeness Corn silage, elemental analysis #2795 Protein (N × 6.25) of maize_silage_milk_ripeness Wheat, whole crop, analysed fresh, van Soest fibre #2648–#2653 TS, VS, protein, cell wall of wheat_whole_plant_silage and cereal_gps_silage Meadow grass #613–#617, #1699, #3193, #3197, #3286 VS, protein of grass_silage and green_rye_silage Grass with detergent fibre #1038, #2377 Cell wall of grass_silage and green_rye_silage Maize grain; shelled corn #1033; #1973 Grain part of corn_cob_mix Corn cob (spindle) #979, #1035, #1037, #1102, #1240, #1454, #2068, #2302, #2791 Spindle part of corn_cob_mix Fresh cattle manure; cow faeces #1882, #2782, #1528; #1391 VS, protein; lipids of both cattle manures Pig manure #1366, #1715, #2246, #3069 TS (#1366), VS, protein of swine_manure Chicken manure, poultry litter 25 samples; #2380; #957 VS, protein; cell wall; lipids of chicken_manure_dry

Samples are left out when they do not describe the material as it is fed: composted or aged manure, digestate, ash, char, pellets, manure with soil or sand bedding. Fibre values are left out when the lignin is a Klason lignin, the method is unknown, or the components add up to more than 100 % of the dry matter. Cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin of a van Soest analysis give NDF (their sum), ADF (cellulose + lignin) and ADL (lignin).

docs.title: Storage state
docs.text:
The storage state describes the substrate as it enters the digester: pH, ammonium, volatile fatty acids, bicarbonate or acid capacity, and temperature. It comes from published analyses of the material, looked up in November 2026:

File pH NH4-N [kg/m³] Acids [g/l] Buffer Temp. [°C] Source cattle_manure 7.4 2.42 6.2 / 1.2 / 0.6 / 0.1 KS43 109 mol/m³ from TIC 10 Overmeyer et al. 2020; pH: Biogashandbuch Bayern swine_manure 7.34 2.88 7.0 / 1.6 / 1.2 / 0.4 KS43 112 mol/m³ from TIC 20 Overmeyer et al. 2020 cattle_manure_solid 7.85 1.59 FFS 6.7 TAC 250 mmol/l 9.3 Mahato et al. 2020 chicken_manure_dry 7.7 3.04 FFS 0 (assumption) TAC 170 mmol/l 9.3 Zhang et al. 2019, scaled to 45 % TS maize_silage_milk_ripeness 3.9 0.17 4.2 / 0 / 0.07 none 9.3 LfL Maissilage 2018 (n = 92) grass_silage 4.6 0.38 6.3 / 0 / 1.9 none 9.3 LfL Grassilage 2018 (n = 82) wheat_whole_plant_silage, cereal_gps_silage 4.0 0.38 7.0 / 0 / 0.4 none 9.3 Leisen 2011, LUFA NRW (n = 20) green_rye_silage 4.45 0.79 1.0 / 0.2 / 0 none 9.3 Zhao et al. 2021 (proxy) corn_cob_mix 4.42 1.24 1.5 / 0.3 / 0 none 9.3 Li et al. 2023 (proxy) onion_waste 5.5 0 (assumption) 0 none 9.3 FDA pH of foods

Acids are acetic / propionic / butyric (/ valeric) acid; FFS is the sum as acetic acid. The conventions behind the table:

  • Slurries: the fresh dairy-cow and fattening-pig slurry of the University of Bonn (Overmeyer et al. 2020, week 0) supplies ammonium, the single acids and the total inorganic carbon of one consistent sample each. KS43 is the bicarbonate share of that inorganic carbon at the slurry pH (pKa 6.35). The pH of the cattle slurry is the one of the Bavarian biogas handbook (7.42 for fresh slurry at 10 % TS); surveys give 7.2 (Petersen et al. 2016, n = 39) and 7.74 (Overmeyer et al. 2020).
  • Solid manures: a measured total alkalinity is written as TAC, from which the loader subtracts the acid anions titrated along. The values of the chicken manure are measured at 33 % TS and scaled to the 45 % TS of the file. The ammonium of the poultry manure is the measured ammonium; the fertiliser reference values (LfL Basisdaten) count 45 % of the nitrogen as ammonium by convention, uric acid included, and are not used.
  • Silages: the laboratories report the fermentation acids in g/kg dry matter and the ammonia nitrogen as a share of the total nitrogen. Both are converted with TS and RP of the file (N = RP / 6.25; 1 kg fresh matter taken as 1 l). Lactic acid is the main fermentation product (maize 45, grass 59 g/kg TS) but has no state in ADM1: it is not written to the file, its COD stays in the carbohydrate pools. A silage below pH 4.3 has no acid capacity by definition. Propionic acid is not reported separately by the German laboratories and is set to zero where it is not measured.
  • Temperature: substrates stored outdoors take the mean air temperature of Germany 1991–2020 (DWD, 9.3 °C). Slurry in cattle houses is 5.5–12.3 °C (Petersen et al. 2016; 10 °C in the file), in pig houses about 20 °C (Ma et al. 2023).
  • Proxies: no open data set for a German green rye silage or corn-cob mix could be found. Green rye carries the fermentation quality of Korean forage rye cut at heading (Zhao et al. 2021), corn-cob mix that of untreated high-moisture ear corn at 63 % DM (Li et al. 2023), which lies within the typical ranges of Kung & Shaver. Both files say so in their comments.

docs.title: What each file rests on
docs.text:
• maize_silage_milk_ripeness: Phyllis. The five hybrids hold 51–73 % cell wall and 8–25 % non-structural carbohydrates, an early, starch-poor harvest. Today's dough-ripe silage holds about 40 % cell wall.
  • wheat_whole_plant_silage, cereal_gps_silage: Phyllis. Wheat is the only whole-crop cereal in the database, so both files share its dry-matter composition and differ in lipids and price only.
  • grass_silage: Phyllis for ash, protein and cell wall. TS is the KTBL standard, because the grass samples were dried.
  • corn_cob_mix: Phyllis holds grain and spindle separately. The file mixes 90 % grain and 10 % spindle; the share is an assumption.
  • cattle_manure, cattle_manure_solid, swine_manure: Phyllis for ash, protein and lipids. The fibre values of the manure samples are unusable (one adds up to 127 % with its ash, the others lack the hemicellulose), so these files keep the crude-fibre route with the crude fibre of the superseded file.
  • chicken_manure_dry: Phyllis, including one van Soest analysis. Protein is N × 6.25 of the dried sample and therefore contains the uric acid.
  • green_rye_silage: no Phyllis sample. The dry-matter composition is the one of grass, as the closest material; the fermentation quality is that of Korean forage rye cut at heading. The weakest file of the library.
  • onion_waste: Phyllis holds onion peel and ash analyses only. The composition of the whole onion comes from the USDA food database; total dietary fibre stands in for the cell wall. Fresh bulbs carry neither ammonium nor fermentation acids; the pH is the one of raw onions.
  • maize_silage_gummersbach, swine_manure_gummersbach: plant-specific files. The laboratory values of the plant are kept; only the degradation level, which had no source, is replaced by the standard methane yield.

Limits of these values

Nitrogen measured on a dried manure sample misses the ammonia lost in drying; protein from it is an estimate. The methane yields are the guide values behind the BiomasseV 2012; the KTBL revised its guide values in 2021 and that edition was not available here. The conversion of the yield to the volatile solids uses the KTBL standard dry matter of each substrate. The storage state of each slurry rests on one fresh sample of one farm; the fatty acids of the dry poultry manure and the ammonium of the onion waste are set to zero for want of a source; green rye and corn-cob mix carry proxies from abroad.

docs.title: ADM1 Implementation and Substrate Modeling
docs.text:
This page describes the technical details of the ADM1 model implemented in PyADM1ODE and how agricultural substrates are integrated into the model.

PyADM1ODE implements ADM1da (Schlattmann 2011) — an agricultural adaptation of the original ADM1 (Batstone et al. 2002, IWA Task Group). Compared to the classical formulation, this model adds sub-fractioned disintegration, temperature-dependent kinetics, and modified inhibition kinetics for agricultural co-digestion. The implementation reproduces the reference behaviour of SIMBA# biogas 4.2 (ifak Magdeburg) quantitatively (see the Validation page). Where the published ADM1da literature is ambiguous on a specific stoichiometric or kinetic choice, the convention followed by PyADM1ODE is stated explicitly throughout this page.

docs.title: ADM1 as a Pure ODE System
docs.text: Unlike the standard ADM1, which is often formulated as a system of differential- algebraic equations (DAE), this implementation is a pure system of ordinary differential equations (ODE).

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
1. Kinetic acid-base equilibrium: the ionised species (acetate, propionate, butyrate, valerate ions, \(\text{HCO}_3^-\), \(\text{NH}_3\)) are carried as dynamic state variables with a very high reaction rate \(k_{A,B} = 10^8\,\text{m}^3\,\text{kmol}^{-1}\,\text{d}^{-1}\). They therefore track the thermodynamic equilibrium essentially in real time, without an algebraic solver having to be invoked inside the ODE step.
  2. Kinetic gas-liquid transfer: \(\text{H}_2\), \(\text{CH}_4\) and \(\text{CO}_2\) are transferred to the gas phase via \(k_L a\) rates — no algebraic Henry equilibrium constraint. Free ammonia leaves with the gas at its equilibrium concentration.
  3. 41 state variables: the model carries 41 variables in five blocks:
Block Indices Count Contents Soluble components 0–11 12 \(S_{su}, S_{aa}, S_{fa}, S_{va}, S_{bu}, S_{pro}, S_{ac}, S_{h2}, S_{ch4}, S_{IC}, S_{IN}, S_{I}\) Particulate sub-fractions 12–21 10 \(X_{PS\_ch/pr/li}\) (slow), \(X_{PF\_ch/pr/li}\) (fast), \(X_{S\_ch/pr/li}\) (hydrolysable), \(X_I\) Biomass 22–28 7 \(X_{su}, X_{aa}, X_{fa}, X_{c4}, X_{pro}, X_{ac}, X_{h2}\) Acid-base / charge balance 29–36 8 \(S_{cat}, S_{an}\), ionised forms \(S_{va^-}, S_{bu^-}, S_{pro^-}, S_{ac^-}, S_{HCO_3^-}, S_{NH_3}\) Gas phase 37–40 4 \(p_{H_2}, p_{CH_4}, p_{CO_2}, p_{tot}\)

docs.title: pH calculation
docs.text:
The pH is determined at every evaluation step from the charge balance using a Newton–Raphson iteration:

\[ S_{cat} - S_{an} + (S_{NH4} - S_{NH3}) - S_{HCO_3^-} - \frac{S_{ac^-}}{64} - \frac{S_{pro^-}}{112} - \frac{S_{bu^-}}{160} - \frac{S_{va^-}}{208} + S_{H^+} - \frac{K_w}{S_{H^+}} = 0 \]

Since every contribution on the left-hand side is a state variable, this charge balance is a purely point-wise function of the current state within the ODE step and converges to \([H^+]\) in 5–10 Newton iterations with high accuracy. The fast equilibration of the ionised species via \(k_{A,B}\) ensures the computed pH stays consistent with the thermodynamic acid-base constants.

docs.title: Sub-fractioned disintegration
docs.text:
The most important difference compared to classical ADM1 is the two-pool disintegration instead of the single composite variable \(X_c\):

                     substrate inflow
                          │
        ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
        │                 │                 │
   X_PS_ch/pr/li      X_PF_ch/pr/li      X_I (inert)
   (slow pool)        (fast pool)
        │                 │
        │ k_dis_PS=0.04   │ k_dis_PF=0.4
        │ d⁻¹             │ d⁻¹
        ▼                 ▼
             X_S_ch/pr/li (hydrolysable)
                   │
                   │ k_hyd ≈ 4 d⁻¹
                   ▼
               S_su / S_aa / S_fa

Routing of the inflow COD to the pools (via Feedstock._calc_concentrations):

Pool Substrate source (Weender + sub-fractioning parameters) \(X_{PS}\) Crude fibre (always slow pool) plus the share \(f_{sOTS}\) of NFE carbohydrates, proteins, and lipids \(X_{PF}\) Share \(f_{fOTS}\) of NFE carbohydrates, proteins, and lipids \(X_S\) Produced by disintegration from \(X_{PS}\) and \(X_{PF}\); never sourced directly from the substrate \(X_I\) Share \(a_{XI}\) of the total raw organic COD \(S_I\) Share \(a_{Si}\) of the total raw organic COD (soluble inerts, appear directly in the inflow)

This makes it possible, for example, to route easily degradable starch (NFE) into the fast pool while lignocellulose (crude fibre) automatically lands in the slow pool — without changing the model structure.

docs.title: Biomass decay routing
docs.text:
When a biomass population \(X_i\) decays, the corresponding COD is routed to the hydrolysable pool \(X_S\) and the inert pool \(X_I\) — not to the slow disintegration pool \(X_{PS}\). This follows the biomass-decay stoichiometry of ADM1da (Schlattmann 2011), where all seven biomass populations decay into the same combination of hydrolysable and inert pools. The COD-basis routing fractions are

\[ f_{CH\_XB} = \frac{f_{BM,CH} \cdot M_{Xch}}{M_{XB}} \approx 0.246, \quad f_{PR\_XB} = \frac{f_{BM,PR} \cdot M_{Xpr}}{M_{XB}} \approx 0.709, \quad f_{LI\_XB} = \frac{f_{BM,LI} \cdot M_{Xli}}{M_{XB}} \approx 0.045 \]

with \(f_{BM,CH} = 0{,}20\), \(f_{BM,PR} = 0{,}70\), \(f_{BM,LI} = 0{,}10\) (biomass mass composition), and \(M_{Xch} = 0{,}9375\), \(M_{Xpr} = 0{,}7736\), \(M_{Xli} = 0{,}3474\) (mass-to-COD ratios). A fraction \(f_P = 0{,}20\) goes to the inert pool \(X_I\); the remaining \((1 - f_P) = 0{,}80\) is split among the \(X_{S,*}\) pools using the COD-basis fractions above. The hydrolysis rate \(k_{hyd} = 4\,\text{d}^{-1}\) is 100× faster than \(k_{dis,PS} = 0{,}04\,\text{d}^{-1}\), so decayed biomass re-enters the substrate chain on the hydrolysis timescale.

The inert share keeps the composition of the biomass, so it holds protein in the same proportion as the degradable share. Biomass carries \(N_{XB} = f_{BM,PR} \cdot N_{aa}\) nitrogen, its decay products \(f_{PR\_XB} \cdot N_{aa}\), with \(N_{aa} = 0.00765\) kmol N per kg COD (13.84 % nitrogen in protein). Decay therefore binds a little ammonium (\(6.9 \cdot 10^{-5}\) kmol N per kg COD) instead of releasing any. Up to version 0.6.2 the inert share had a lower nitrogen content; decay then released nitrogen and left about 2 % more ammonium in the digester.

docs.title: Temperature-dependent kinetics
docs.text:
The ADM1da variant corrects every kinetic rate against the 35 °C reference using an Arrhenius-θ function:

\[ k(T) = k(35\,°\text{C}) \cdot \theta^{(T[°\text{C}] - 35)} \]

with group-specific exponents (values after Schlattmann 2011):

Process group \(\theta_{\exp}\) Disintegration & hydrolysis 0.024 \(X_{su}, X_{aa}, X_{h2}\) (growth & decay) 0.069 \(X_{fa}, X_{c4}, X_{pro}, X_{ac}\) (growth & decay) 0.055 \(K_{I,NH_3,X_{pro}}\) 0.061 \(K_{I,NH_3,X_{ac}}\) 0.086 \(K_{I,H_2,X_{fa}/X_{c4}/X_{pro}}\) 0.080

The correction is applied once when the ADM1 object is created — to all relevant rates via ADMParams.apply_temperature_corrections — and cached in the internal _kinetic dict.

docs.title: Modified inhibition kinetics
docs.text:
Compared to the standard ADM1, the ADM1da model includes the following adjustments — all implemented in ADM1.ADM_ODE following the ADM1da uptake- process rate laws (Schlattmann 2011), with the NH₃-inhibition forms taken from Siegrist et al. (2002):

Inhibition Standard ADM1 ADM1da (this implementation) pH inhibition \(X_{su}/X_{aa}/X_{fa}/X_{c4}/X_{pro}\) Hill, \(n=1\) Hill, \(n=2\) (sharper cut-off) pH inhibition \(X_{ac}\) Hill, \(n=1\) Hill, \(n=3\) pH inhibition \(X_{h2}\) Hill, \(n=1\) Hill, \(n=3\) \(\text{NH}_3\) inhibition \(X_{ac}\) linear in \(S_{NH3}\) squared Hill: \(K_I^2/(K_I^2 + S_{NH3}^2)\), T-corrected with \(\theta=0.086\) \(\text{NH}_3\) inhibition \(X_{pro}\) not present squared Hill with own \(K_{I,nh3,pro}\), T-corrected with \(\theta=0.061\) Undissociated propionate \(X_{pro}\) not present \(K_{IH,pro}/(K_{IH,pro} + S_{pro} - S_{pro^-})\) Undissociated acetate \(X_{ac}\) not present \(K_{IH,ac}/(K_{IH,ac} + S_{ac} - S_{ac^-})\) \(\text{CO}_2\) limitation \(X_{h2}\) not present squared Hill saturation: \(S_{CO2}^2/(K_S^2 + S_{CO2}^2)\) with the dissolved \(S_{CO2} = S_{IC} - S_{HCO_3^-}\)

Inhibition scope

The ADM1da kinetics as published in Schlattmann (2011) list an acetate / undissociated-acid inhibition term on \(X_{fa}\) and \(X_{c4}\) as well. The SIMBA# reference implementation and PyADM1ODE apply these terms only to \(X_{pro}\) and \(X_{ac}\), where they are well-supported by experimental data; \(X_{fa}\) and \(X_{c4}\) are inhibited only by pH, N-limitation, and dissolved H₂.

These extensions reproduce the behaviour typically observed in agricultural plants: a sharper pH drop on acid accumulation, more pronounced \(\text{NH}_3\) inhibition under thermophilic manure-based operation, and more realistic propionate dynamics.

docs.title: Acid-base sub-system
docs.text:
The acid-base reactions of the six dissociating species (\(\text{NH}_4^+ / \text{NH}_3\), \(\text{CO}_2 / \text{HCO}_3^-\), and the four VFA pairs) are implemented as kinetic reactions of the form

\[ \rho_{A,i} = k_{A,B} \cdot \left( S_{i^-} \cdot S_{H^+} - K_{a,i} \cdot (S_i - S_{i^-}) \right), \quad i \in \{ \text{va}, \text{bu}, \text{pro}, \text{ac} \} \]

with the same kinetic coupling for \(\text{CO}_2 / \text{HCO}_3^-\) and \(\text{NH}_4^+ / \text{NH}_3\). A pair settles at the rate \(k_{A,B} \cdot (S_{H^+} + K_a)\). With \(k_{A,B} = 10^8\,\text{m}^3\,\text{kmol}^{-1}\,\text{d}^{-1}\) and pH 7.4 the VFA pairs settle within a minute, \(\text{CO}_2 / \text{HCO}_3^-\) within half an hour and \(\text{NH}_4^+ / \text{NH}_3\) within a few hours, which is fast against the biology. The acid dissociation constants are T-corrected against the 25 °C reference using van't Hoff with the enthalpies from Batstone 2002:

\[ K_a(T) = K_a(298\,\text{K}) \cdot \exp\left(\frac{\Delta H^\circ}{R} \cdot \left(\frac{1}{298} - \frac{1}{T}\right)\right) \]

\(S_{IC}\) (S_co2) and \(S_{IN}\) (S_nh4) are totals: bicarbonate and free ammonia are subsets of them, as the term \(S_i - S_{i^-}\) of the rate shows. An acid-base reaction only shifts between the two forms, so \(\rho_A\) appears in the balance of the ionised form alone and not in the balance of the total. Carbon and nitrogen are conserved this way; up to version 0.6.2 the rate was also added to the two totals, which removed about 4 % of the ammonium and 2 % of the gas carbon from the balance.

docs.title: Gas-liquid transfer (Henry's law with van't Hoff correction)
docs.text:
The three gas-phase species \(\text{H}_2\), \(\text{CH}_4\) and \(\text{CO}_2\) are transferred between the liquid and gas phases via

\[ r_{F,gas} = k_L a_F \cdot \left( S_F - \frac{p_F}{K_H(T)\,R\,T} \right) \cdot \frac{V_{liq}}{V_{gas}} \]

with a van't Hoff temperature correction of the Henry constant (Schlattmann 2011 / Batstone et al. 2002 enthalpies):

\[ H_F(T) = H_F(T_{ref}) \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{\Delta H^\circ_F}{R} \cdot \left(\frac{1}{T_{ref}} - \frac{1}{T}\right)\right) \] Gas \(H_{F,25°C}\) [mol/(L·bar)] \(\Delta H^\circ_F\) [J/mol] \(k_L a_F\) [d⁻¹] CO₂ 0.035 19 410 200 CH₄ 0.0014 14 240 200 H₂ 7.8·10⁻⁴ 4 180 200 NH₃ 60 36 584 – (see below)

Sign convention: dissolution is exothermic, so \(H_F\) decreases as \(T\) rises — less gas remains dissolved at higher operating temperature.

docs.title: Ammonia in the gas
docs.text: Ammonia is over a thousand times more soluble than \(\text{CO}_2\), so its gas concentration follows the liquid without delay: the headspace holds \(S_{NH_3} / (H_{NH_3}\,R\,T)\) kmol N per m³. This ammonia leaves with the gas flow and is taken from \(S_{IN}\) and \(S_{NH_3}\); there is no separate gas-phase state for it. At 42 °C and 115 mg/l of free ammonia nitrogen the dry gas carries about 300 ppm, just under 1 % of the inorganic nitrogen of a maize and manure digester.

docs.title: Headspace pressure
docs.text:
The gas leaves through an outlet at the rate \(k_p \cdot (p_{dry} + p_{H_2O} - p_{ext})\). The wet headspace therefore settles at the pressure \(p_{ext}\) it vents against, and the dry gas holds \(p_{ext} - p_{H_2O}\): 0.93 bar at 42 °C with the default \(p_{ext} = 1.013\) bar. A gas system with back pressure is set through ADM1.p_ext.

The dry gas pressure sets the dissolved \(\text{CO}_2\) and with it the pH. Up to version 0.6.2 the water vapour pressure was subtracted twice, which left the dry gas at 0.85 bar and the dissolved \(\text{CO}_2\) about 9 % too low.

docs.title: Reported gas flows
docs.text:
Q_gas, Q_ch4 and Q_co2 are dry gas at standard conditions (0 °C, 1.01325 bar; DIN 1343), in Nm³/d:

  • The flows are the ones the gas-phase ODE removes from the headspace, split by the dry partial pressures. Methane, carbon dioxide and hydrogen add up to Q_gas, and the methane flow closes the COD balance.
  • The headspace is saturated with water vapour. It adds to the pressure that drives the outflow, but it is not part of Q_gas; ADM1.calc_gas() returns it separately as q_h2o.
  • The reference volume is the one BMP uses (22.414 Nm³ per kmol), so a methane yield and a methane potential can be compared directly.
  • Q_ch4 / Q_gas is the methane content of the dry gas, which is what a gas analyser shows.

Up to version 0.6.2 the flows were given at 20 °C with the water vapour counted inside Q_gas. Against those numbers Q_gas is about 7 % lower, the methane content about 4 percentage points higher and Q_ch4 about 1 % higher (at 40 °C).

docs.title: Sludge-volume balance and HRT
docs.text:
Because a significant fraction of the substrate COD leaves the reactor as gas, the sludge volume is not conserved. Every organic fraction takes up the volume \(v_i = iM_i / \rho_i\) per kg COD (mass-to-COD ratio over density); hydrogen, methane and inorganic carbon take up none. The sludge loses the net volume of what the conversions turn over:

\[ \frac{dV_S}{dt} = \dot{q}_{S,in} - \dot{q}_{S,out} - \dot{q}_{S,loss}, \quad \dot{q}_{S,loss} = -V_S \cdot \sum_j \rho_j \sum_i \nu_{ij} \cdot v_i \]

with the rate \(\rho_j\) of process \(j\) and its stoichiometric coefficients \(\nu_{ij}\).

Fraction \(iM\) [kg/kg COD] \(\rho\) [kg/m³] Carbohydrates, sugars 0.9375 1550 Proteins, amino acids 0.7736 1370 Lipids, fatty acids 0.3474 920 Valerate / butyrate / propionate / acetate 0.490 / 0.550 / 0.661 / 0.9375 940 / 960 / 990 / 1050 Biomass 0.7638 1361

Disintegration and the hydrolysis of carbohydrates and proteins keep the volume; most of it is lost where acetate becomes methane. At steady state the loss is about 0.59 litres per kg COD of methane formed, the ratio SIMBA# determines for its reactors. Up to version 0.6.2 the loss was taken from the hydrolysis rates alone, which gave about 10 % more.

The hydraulic retention time follows a first-order lag (Schlattmann 2011):

\[ \frac{dHRT}{dt} + HRT \cdot \frac{\dot{q}_{S,in}}{V_S} = 1, \quad HRT_{ss} = \frac{V_S}{\dot{q}_{S,in}} \]

The effluent is driven by an overflow weir at \(V_{liq,max}\) with a small time constant \(\tau_{out}\):

\[ \dot{q}_{S,out} = \max\!\left( 0,\; \frac{V_S - V_{liq,max}}{\tau_{out}} \right) \]

In practice \(\tau_{out} = 0{,}05\,\text{d}\) pins \(V_S\) within ~1 m³ of the setpoint, reproducing SIMBA#'s essentially-instantaneous weir behaviour.

When dynamic_volume=False (default for backward compatibility), \(V_S\) is held constant and \(\dot{q}_{S,out} = \dot{q}_{S,in} - \dot{q}_{S,loss}\) is computed directly from the mass loss term.

docs.title: Substrate characterization via Weender analysis
docs.text:
Substrates are defined via common laboratory parameters and stored as YAML files under data/substrates/. The standard schema, after SIMBA, has this structure (the superseded legacy/maize_silage_milk_ripeness.yaml):

name: Maize silage (milk ripeness)

TS:     330.0     # kg/m^3 FM   total solids
NH4:      0.8     # kg N/m^3 FM ammonia nitrogen
BGP:    670.0     # Nm^3/t VS   biogas potential
BMP:    356.8     # Nm^3 CH4/t VS  biomethane potential

aXI:      0.1029  # particulate inert fraction of degradable COD
fOTSrf:   0.95    # biodegradable fraction of crude fibre
fsOTS:    0.0     # share of degradable VS into slow pool (XPS)
ffOTS:    1.0     # share of degradable VS into fast pool (XPF)
aSi:      0.0     # dissolved inert fraction of degradable COD

fRF:      0.235   # crude fibre   (fraction of TS)
fRP:      0.09    # crude protein
fRFe:     0.03    # crude lipid
fRA:      0.10    # ash

Temp:    20.0     # degC
pH:       4.0
KS43:     0.0     # mol/m^3   acid capacity to pH 4.3
FFS:      5.0     # kg HAc/m^3 VFAs as acetic-acid equivalent

The same file may instead be written as XML or TOML; the loader dispatches on the extension. See data/substrates/examples/ for parallel examples in all three formats.

A substrate may also be described by measured laboratory values instead of the COD fractionation (cell-wall analysis NDF / ADL, protein bound in the cell wall NDICP, methane potential BMP or degradation level D_VS, single acids, titrated acid capacity). The bundled substrate files are written this way. See Measured parameters.

load_substrate() returns a SubstrateParams dataclass; the Feedstock class derives from it the full 38-column ADM1 inflow stream (37 liquid state columns + Q):

  1. Fresh-matter density \(\rho_{FM}\) from the component densities (specific-volume mixing rule).
  2. Organic COD concentrations \(X_{ch}, X_{pr}, X_{li}\) in \(\text{kg COD/m}^3\) via the COD conversion factors \(M_{Xch}, M_{Xpr}, M_{Xli}\).
  3. Routing into the sub-fractions \(X_{PS}/X_{PF}\) via \(f_{sOTS}, f_{fOTS}\), and \(f_{OTSrf}\) (see the table above).
  4. Dissociation at the substrate pH: ionised VFAs, \(\text{HCO}_3^-\), \(\text{NH}_3\).
  5. Charge balance for the ions, closed by the strong ions and split by sign: a net-anionic material (silage at its own pH) carries the excess as \(S_{anion}\), a net-cationic one (slurry, solid manure, where \(\text{HCO}_3^-\) and the VFA anions exceed \(\text{NH}_4^+\)) as \(S_{cation}\) — the strong-base cations K⁺, Na⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ of the material. Both pools stay non-negative. Only the difference \(S_{cation} - S_{anion}\) enters pH, speciation and the acid capacity, so the chemistry equals the ADM1da closure (Schlattmann 2011: \(S_{cation} \equiv 0\), \(S_{anion}\) signed); the split keeps the influent inside the non-negative state box that state estimators clip to.

docs.title: Volumetric ADM1da convention for Q
docs.text:
Substrate volumetric flows \(Q_i\) are interpreted as mass-equivalent flows by default. Internally,

\[ Q_{actual,i} = Q_{input,i} \cdot \frac{1000}{\rho_{FM,i}} \]

is computed. For liquid substrates (\(\rho_{FM} \approx 1000\)) this is a no-op; for maize silage (\(\rho_{FM} \approx 1129\,\text{kg/m}^3\)) the actual volumetric flow shrinks by roughly 11 %. This reproduces the behaviour of ADM1da reference results. Setting simba_q_convention=False disables the scaling — useful when \(Q\) should be interpreted directly as the actual reactor volume.

docs.title: Co-digestion: weighted blending
docs.text: For multi-substrate inflows, concentrations are blended by volumetric flow (Feedstock._blended_concentrations). The number of simultaneously fed substrates is unbounded — Feedstock accepts an arbitrarily long list of XML IDs.

docs.title: Measurement outputs
docs.text: PyADM1ODE exposes the standard ADM1da measurement outputs (Schlattmann 2011) for plant-monitoring use cases.

docs.title: Volatile fatty acids (VFA)
docs.text:
The aggregate VFA value in g HAc/L is the COD-weighted acetic-acid equivalent of the four VFA species:

\[ \text{VFA} = M_{HAc} \cdot \sum_i \frac{S_i}{\text{COD}_{MOL,i}}, \quad i \in \{ \text{va}, \text{bu}, \text{pro}, \text{ac} \} \]

with \(M_{HAc} = 60\,\text{g/mol}\) and per-VFA COD-per-mol ratios (va = 208, bu = 160, pro = 112, ac = 64 g COD/mol).

docs.title: Acid capacity (TAC)
docs.text:
The pH 5 titration capacity (TAC, in g CaCO₃/L) is

\[ \text{TAC} = 50 \cdot \Bigl[ \left(F_{NH_3} - K_{A,NH_4} \cdot \frac{F_{NH_4} + F_{NH_3}}{10^{-pH_5} + K_{A,NH_4}}\right) + \left(F_{HCO_3} - K_{A,CO_2} \cdot \frac{F_{CO_2} + F_{HCO_3}}{10^{-pH_5} + K_{A,CO_2}}\right) + \sum_{i = \text{va},\text{bu},\text{pro},\text{ac}} (\cdots) + F_{AN} - F_{CAT} \Bigr] \]

Convention: the ion term is the strong-ion difference

The term \(F_{AN} - F_{CAT}\) subtracts the strong-ion difference \(S_{cation} - S_{anion}\), which the substrate characterisation closes from the charge balance (split by sign, both pools non-negative — the same chemistry as the ADM1da closure with \(S_{cation} \equiv 0\)). A state whose strong-ion difference does not match its weak-acid buffer therefore reports too little acid capacity — negative in the extreme. The pre-inoculated initial state is closed the same way, and tanks without a substrate feed of their own (post-digesters, stores) are seeded with the ammonium of the ADM1da reference inoculum rather than with zero nitrogen. Should the formula still yield \(\text{TAC} \le 0\), PyADM1ODE reports NaN and warns once — this keeps FOS/TAC from exploding on a denominator drifting through zero.

Prefactor 50 vs 100

The TAC formula as written in Schlattmann (2011) uses the molar mass of CaCO₃ (100 kg/kmol) as prefactor. The physically correct value is the equivalent weight 50 kg/keq, because one mole of CaCO₃ carries two H⁺-equivalents of acid-neutralising capacity — the standard alkalinity convention. PyADM1ODE applies the equivalent-weight prefactor, which matches the reference numerical output of the SIMBA# reactor module.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
The implementation builds on the following primary sources (matching the citation list of the PyADM1ODE–SIMBA# validation report):

  • Batstone, D. J., Keller, J., Angelidaki, I., Kalyuzhnyi, S. V., Pavlostathis, S. G., Rozzi, A., Sanders, W. T. M., Siegrist, H., Vavilin, V. A. (2002). Anaerobic Digestion Model No. 1 (ADM1). IWA Scientific and Technical Report No. 13. IWA Publishing, London.
  • Henneberg, W., Strohmann, F. (1864). Beiträge zur Begründung einer rationellen Fütterung der Wiederkäuer. Schwetschke, Braunschweig. (Origin of the Weender feed analysis used for substrate characterisation.)
  • Schlattmann, M. (2011). Weiterentwicklung des Anaerobic Digestion Model No. 1 (ADM1) zur Anwendung auf landwirtschaftliche Substrate. Dissertation, Technische Universität München.
  • Siegrist, H., Vogt, D., Garcia-Heras, J. L., Gujer, W. (2002). Mathematical Model for Meso- and Thermophilic Anaerobic Sewage Sludge Digestion. Environmental Science & Technology 36(5), 1113–1123.

docs.title: Technical implementation
docs.text:
The whole model is pure Python:

Module Purpose pyadm1.core.adm1 ADM1 class with ADM_ODE, Newton–Raphson pH, gas output pyadm1.core.adm_params Stoichiometry, kinetics, inhibition, \(\theta\) corrections pyadm1.core.solver Wrapper around scipy.integrate.solve_ivp (BDF, adaptive) pyadm1.substrates.feedstock XML parser, sub-fractioning routing, blending pyadm1.components.biological.digester Component wrapper with sludge volume and HRT logic

The simulation runs in any standard Python environment and works equally well in containers, web notebooks (Colab), and CI pipelines.

docs.title: Rate-family hook
docs.text:
ADM1.rate_hook lets an outside model rescale the kinetic rates without touching balances or stoichiometry. It is None by default, which leaves ADM_ODE unchanged. When set, it is called once per right-hand-side evaluation as rate_hook(state, S_H, q_ad) and must return 13 factors in the order of pyadm1.core.adm1.RATE_FAMILIES:

dis_PS, dis_PF, hyd_ch, hyd_pr, hyd_li, su, aa, fa, c4, pro, ac, h2, dec

Each factor multiplies every rate of its family (for example c4 scales the valerate and the butyrate uptake, dec all seven decay rates). The torch backend applies the same factors: adm1da_rhs_torch(x, p, rate_factors) takes a (…, 13) tensor and stays differentiable in it, and make_scipy_rhs calls the hook like the numpy path. Typical uses are sensitivity studies of the rate families and hybrid models that correct the kinetics of one plant.

docs.title: Advanced Features
docs.text: PyADM1ODE provides advanced features for large-scale studies and configuration management.

docs.title: Parallel Simulation
docs.text:
Run multiple scenarios concurrently to speed up parameter sweeps or Monte Carlo simulations.

from pyadm1.simulation import ParallelSimulator

# Parameter sweep
parallel = ParallelSimulator(adm1, n_workers=4)
scenarios = [
    {"k_dis_PF": 0.5, "Q": [15, 10, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]},
    {"k_dis_PF": 0.6, "Q": [15, 10, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]},
    {"k_dis_PF": 0.7, "Q": [15, 10, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]}
]

results = parallel.run_scenarios(scenarios, duration=30, initial_state=state)

See the Parallel Simulation Example for more details.

docs.title: Configuration Management
docs.text:
Save and reuse plant designs using JSON serialization.

# Save configuration
plant.to_json("two_stage_plant.json")

# Load later
from pyadm1.configurator import BiogasPlant
plant = BiogasPlant.from_json("two_stage_plant.json", feedstock)
plant.initialize()
results = plant.simulate(duration=30, dt=1/24)

docs.title: PyADM1ODE Ecosystem
docs.text:
PyADM1ODE is part of a larger ecosystem of tools for biogas plant optimization and control:

  • PyADM1ODE_calibration: Tools for automated calibration of ADM1 parameters based on measurement data.
  • PyADM1ODE_mcp: Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that enables controlling PyADM1ODE with LLMs (like Claude or ChatGPT).
  • PyADM1ODE_estimate: Tools for real-time estimation of state variables and parameters.

docs.title: Typical Applications
docs.text: PyADM1ODE can be used for a wide range of tasks, from plant design to real-time optimization.

docs.title: 1. Plant Design and Optimization
docs.text:
Test different plant configurations to find the optimal setup for your needs.

from pyadm1.configurator import BiogasPlant, PlantConfigurator
from pyadm1.substrates import Feedstock

# Test different digester sizes
for V_liq in [1500, 2000, 2500]:
    plant = BiogasPlant(f"Plant_{V_liq}")
    feedstock = Feedstock()
    configurator = PlantConfigurator(plant, feedstock)
    configurator.add_digester("dig1", V_liq=V_liq, Q_substrates=[15, 10, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0])

    plant.initialize()
    results = plant.simulate(duration=30, dt=1/24)

    final = results[-1]["components"]["dig1"]
    print(f"V={V_liq} m³ → CH4={final['Q_ch4']:.1f} m³/d")

docs.title: 2. Substrate Optimization
docs.text:
Compare different substrate mixes to maximize methane production or minimize costs.

# Compare different substrate mixes
mixes = {
    'high_energy': [20, 5, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0],
    'balanced': [15, 10, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0],
    'waste_based': [0, 15, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 10, 5]
}

for name, Q in mixes.items():
    # ... configure and simulate ...
    print(f"{name}: {final['Q_ch4']:.1f} m³/d methane")

docs.title: 3. Energy Balance Analysis
docs.text:
Analyze the net energy production and parasitic loads of your plant.

from pyadm1.components.mechanical import Pump

# Plant with a CHP, a mixer and a pump
plant = BiogasPlant("Energy_Balance")
configurator = PlantConfigurator(plant, Feedstock())
configurator.add_digester("dig1", V_liq=2000, Q_substrates=[15, 10, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0])
configurator.add_chp("chp_main", P_el_nom=500)
configurator.auto_connect_digester_to_chp("dig1", "chp_main")
configurator.add_mixer("mixer_1", "dig1")
plant.add_component(Pump("pump_1", Q_nom=25.0))

plant.initialize()
results = plant.simulate(duration=30, dt=1/24)

# Calculate net energy production
chp_power = results[-1]["components"]["chp_main"]["P_el"]
mixer_power = results[-1]["components"]["mixer_1"]["P_consumed"]
pump_power = results[-1]["components"]["pump_1"]["P_consumed"]

parasitic_load = mixer_power + pump_power
net_power = chp_power - parasitic_load

print(f"Net power: {net_power:.1f} kW")
print(f"Parasitic ratio: {parasitic_load/chp_power:.1%}")

docs.title: 4. Two-Stage Process Design
docs.text:
Model advanced plant designs like Temperature-Phased Anaerobic Digestion (TPAD).

# Temperature-phased anaerobic digestion (TPAD)
configurator.add_digester("hydrolysis", V_liq=500, T_ad=318.15)  # 45°C
configurator.add_digester("main", V_liq=2000, T_ad=308.15)       # 35°C
configurator.connect("hydrolysis", "main", "liquid")

# Enhanced hydrolysis in stage 1, stable methanogenesis in stage 2

docs.title: Research Applications
docs.text:
This framework supports research in:

  • Process optimization: Substrate feed strategies, retention time.
  • Control systems: Model predictive control, feedback controllers.
  • Plant design: Component sizing, layout optimization.
  • Energy management: CHP scheduling, heat integration.
  • Substrate evaluation: Biogas potential assessment.

docs.title: Installation Guide
docs.text: This guide covers the installation of PyADM1ODE on different operating systems.

docs.title: Minimum Requirements
docs.text:
• Python: 3.10 or higher
  • Operating System: Windows, Linux, or macOS
  • Memory: 2 GB RAM minimum (4 GB recommended)
  • Disk Space: 10 MB for installation

PyADM1ODE is pure Python with no native runtime dependencies — installing the Python package is enough.

docs.title: Method 1: Install from GitHub with pip
docs.text:
The package is not on PyPI. pip installs it straight from the repository:

pip install git+https://github.com/dgaida/PyADM1ODE.git

The distribution and the import name are both pyadm1.

docs.title: Method 2: Install from Source
docs.text:
For development or the latest features:

# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/dgaida/PyADM1ODE.git
cd PyADM1ODE

# Install in development mode
pip install -e .

docs.title: Method 3: Using Conda
docs.text:
Create a dedicated environment:

# Create environment from environment.yml
conda env create -f environment.yml

# Activate the environment
conda activate biogas

# Install PyADM1
pip install -e .

docs.title: Windows Installation
docs.text:
1. Install Python (if not already installed):
  2. Download from python.org

  3. Ensure "Add Python to PATH" is checked during installation

  4. Install PyADM1: 

    pip install git+https://github.com/dgaida/PyADM1ODE.git
# or from source:
git clone https://github.com/dgaida/PyADM1ODE.git
cd PyADM1ODE
pip install -e .

    python -c "import pyadm1; print(pyadm1.__version__)"

docs.title: Linux Installation (Ubuntu/Debian)

1. Install Python and dependencies: 

    sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install python3 python3-pip

  2. Install PyADM1ODE:

# or from source:
git clone https://github.com/dgaida/PyADM1ODE.git

docs.title: macOS Installation

numpy>=1.20.0         # Numerical computing

docs.title: Quick Verification
docs.text:
Run this Python script to verify all components:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Verify PyADM1 installation."""

def verify_installation():
    """Check all PyADM1 components."""

    # 1. Check core import
    try:
        import pyadm1
        print(f"✓ PyADM1 version: {pyadm1.__version__}")
    except ImportError as e:
        print(f"✗ Failed to import pyadm1: {e}")
        return False

    # 2. Check core modules
    try:
        from pyadm1.core import ADM1
        from pyadm1.substrates import Feedstock
        from pyadm1.simulation import Simulator
        print("✓ Core modules imported successfully")
    except ImportError as e:
        print(f"✗ Failed to import core modules: {e}")
        return False

    # 3. Load a feedstock from the bundled substrate library
    try:
        feedstock = Feedstock(["maize_silage_milk_ripeness", "swine_manure"],
                              feeding_freq=24)
        print("✓ Feedstock loaded from data/substrates/")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"✗ Feedstock load failed: {e}")
        return False

    # 4. Quick simulation test
    try:
        from pyadm1.core.adm1 import ADM1, STATE_SIZE
        adm1 = ADM1(feedstock, V_liq=2000, T_ad=308.15)
        initial_state = [0.01] * STATE_SIZE  # 41-state ADM1da vector
        adm1.create_influent([15, 10], 0)
        print(f"✓ Basic simulation setup works ({STATE_SIZE} states)")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"✗ Simulation test failed: {e}")
        return False

    print("\n✅ All verification checks passed!")
    return True

if __name__ == "__main__":
    verify_installation()

Save as verify_install.py and run: 

python verify_install.py

docs.title: 1. "ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pyadm1'"
docs.text:
Problem: Python can't locate the package.

Solution: Make sure the package is installed in the active environment: 

pip show pyadm1ode
# If empty, install from source:
git clone https://github.com/dgaida/PyADM1ODE.git
cd PyADM1ODE
pip install -e .

docs.title: 2. Substrate file not found
docs.text:
Problem: Feedstock([...]) fails because a substrate ID is unknown.

Solution: Substrate IDs are file stems under data/substrates/ (YAML, XML, or TOML — any supported format). List them: 

ls data/substrates/
Use those filenames (without the extension) as substrate IDs.
